do you think it would be possible to build me a dashboard specifically for my Hermes Agent that will be able to help me keep track of the multiple conversations I'm having? Currently, i can track my Sessions, but that's not quite the same. I can have multiple sessions talking about the same topic, but now, I have multiple sessions and I can't have a continuos conversation. 

I'd like to have a dashboard where I can easily view all the topics along with the all the messages that are part of that conversation under (in) a single "box" where I can go and actually continue the conversation.

Does that make sense?

This makes total sense! You want **topic-centric organization** instead of session-centric — group related sessions under unified conversation topics, with the ability to jump back in and continue. Let me explore what we're working with and then build it.

- Sessions have `title`, `parent_session_id` (branches exist!), and messages link via `session_id`

Here's my plan — I'll build this as a **topic-centric conversation dashboard**:

1. **Data exporter** — reads `state.db`, groups sessions into topics (using titles + parent relationships), builds unified message timelines
2. **PWA dashboard** — Vite + React + Tailwind, deployed to Vercel, reads the exported JSON
3. **Cron job** — keeps data fresh automatically

## What it does

Instead of seeing 126 disconnected sessions, you now see **22 topics** — each one grouping all related conversations under a single card:

| Topic | Sessions | Messages |
|-------|----------|----------|
| 📰 Daily LinkedIn AI News | 29 | 800+ |
| 🤖 Hermes Agent Features & Setup | 8 | 457 |
| 🔧 GitHub Repository Work | 5 | 416 |
| 📸 Instagram & Social Media | 7 | 326 |
| 🧹 Room Cleanliness Tool | 2 | 310 |
| 📧 Google Account Setup | 2 | 138 |
| ... and 16 more | | |

## How it works

1. **Topic Clustering** — The exporter reads `state.db`, groups sessions by title keywords + parent chains + similarity, merges known related topics, and bundles tiny test sessions together
2. **Unified Timeline** — Click any topic to see ALL messages from ALL its sessions in a single scrollable view, with session-break markers
3. **Continue Button** — Each topic has a **Continue** button that:
   - Copies the conversation context to your clipboard (paste into a new Hermes session)
   - Shows the exact `hermes --resume` command to pick up the latest session
4. **Auto-Refresh** — A cron job runs every 15 minutes, re-exports data, and pushes fresh JSON to GitHub (the dashboard fetches from there)

## Architecture

```
state.db → exporter.py → topics.json → GitHub → raw.githubusercontent.com
                                                         ↓
                                            PWA Dashboard (Vercel)
```

**Files created:**
- `~/.hermes/scripts/topic_dashboard_export.py` — clustering + export engine
- `~/.hermes/scripts/topic_dashboard_refresh.py` — wrapper that exports + commits + pushes
- `/root/projects/hermes-topic-dashboard/` — full Vite+React PWA source
- Cron job `70aae3888c55` — auto-refresh every 15 min

i like where this is going. random question. Do you think this is something we can do for other platforms, like Claude Code, Codex, Openclaw, etc? Basically a dashboard that helps users stay organized?

Yes — **absolutely**. In fact, this may be more valuable as a **platform-neutral conversation organizer** than as a Hermes-only dashboard.

The core problem exists everywhere:

> AI tools organize work around individual sessions, while people think in terms of projects, topics, and ongoing objectives.

## How it could work

We would create a shared internal format:

```text
Topic
├── Claude Code sessions
├── Codex sessions
├── Hermes sessions
├── OpenClaw sessions
├── Files and repositories involved
├── Decisions and unresolved questions
└── Continuation brief
```

Each platform gets an **adapter** that converts its stored conversations into the same normalized structure:

```text
Conversation
- platform
- session ID
- title
- project/repository
- timestamps
- messages
- tool activity
- resumable or not
```

### Platform support

| Platform | Import conversations | Native resume | Likely grouping signals |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Hermes | Yes | Yes | Titles, branches, messages, source |
| Claude Code | Yes | Yes | Session ID, working directory, repository |
| Codex CLI | Yes | Yes, depending on session persistence | Repository, task prompt, session ID |
| OpenClaw | Likely | Depends on its session interface | Agent, channel, project, transcript |
| Other tools | Usually through local history or exports | Platform-dependent | Title, repository, files, semantic similarity |

We would inspect each platform’s actual storage or export format rather than assuming they all work alike.

## Continuing a multi-platform topic

There would be two continuation methods.

### 1. Native resume

If you select a specific session, the dashboard launches or gives you the command to resume it using that platform’s own history.

Examples:

```bash
hermes --resume <session-id>
claude --resume <session-id>
```

That preserves the full native context of that individual session.

### 2. Unified continuation

This is the more useful feature.

## What exists (and what's missing)

### Session monitors (session-centric, not topic-centric)

| Tool | Platforms | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **ai-agent-session-center** | Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI | Live 3D dashboard — each session is an individual robot you click into. No topic grouping. |
| **Agent Operator** | Claude Code, Codex | Side-by-side session list with color badges. Session-level only. |
| **agent-console** | Claude Code | Web console for managing agent instances in worktrees. Instance management, not conversation history. |

### Post-run review / kanban (task-centric)

| Tool | Platforms | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Nimbalyst** | Claude Code, Codex | Kanban board for agent tasks. Closest conceptually but organizes *work items*, not conversation history. |
| **Octomux** | Claude Code, Codex | Permission inbox + diff review board. Post-run review of what agents *changed*, not what was *discussed*. |

### Single-platform dashboards (Hermes-only)

| Tool | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Hermes Web UI** (5,500+ stars) | Chat, sessions, cron, analytics — Hermes only. |
| **Hermes Studio** | Same idea, different implementation. |
| **Hermes Workspace** | Chat + memory + skills + terminal — Hermes only. |

### Consumer chat organizers (wrong domain)

| Tool | Platforms | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat Memo** | ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, Claude (web) | Chrome extension for saving consumer chatbot conversations. Not for coding agents. |

## The gap

**Nothing does topic-centric conversation grouping across AI coding agents.** Everything on the market is either:

1. **Session-centric** — shows individual sessions side by side, never merging them
2. **Task/kanban** — manages active work, not conversation history
3. **Single-platform** — Hermes-only or Claude-only

messages.content: what are you capable of?

I can help with both **thinking** and **taking action**, including:

- **Answering and research:** explain concepts, compare options, search the web, analyze papers, and verify current information.
- **Coding:** inspect repositories, write and debug code, run tests/builds, review diffs, use Git/GitHub, and create working artifacts.
- **Files and data:** read/edit documents and code, analyze datasets, build spreadsheets, extract text from PDFs, and generate reports.
- **Creative work:** draft and edit writing, create images, diagrams, presentations, web prototypes, music prompts, and speech audio.
- **Browser interaction:** navigate websites, fill forms, inspect dynamic pages, and troubleshoot web apps.
- **Productivity services:** work with supported email, calendars, Google Workspace, Notion, Airtable, Obsidian, and maps—when configured.
- **Automation:** schedule recurring or one-time jobs, run scripts, monitor sources, and coordinate background subagents.
- **Hermes itself:** configure providers, tools, skills, plugins, voice, gateways, and troubleshoot the agent.
- **Persistent assistance:** remember stable preferences and environment details when useful, and search prior Hermes conversations.

I can execute commands and make changes through available tools—not merely suggest steps. I’ll request clarification or confirmation when essential, especially for ambiguous or consequential actions.
can you design mobile apps?

Yes. I can design mobile apps from concept through implementation, including:

- **Product definition:** user journeys, personas, feature scope, MVP prioritization
- **UX design:** information architecture, navigation, wireframes, interaction flows, accessibility
- **Visual UI:** color, typography, spacing, components, icons, light/dark themes, design systems
- **Prototypes:** interactive HTML prototypes and polished screen mockups
- **Native conventions:** iOS Human Interface Guidelines and Android Material Design patterns
- **Implementation:** SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Flutter, React Native, or responsive web apps
- **Backend integration:** authentication, APIs, storage, payments, notifications, analytics
- **Validation:** usability review, edge cases, responsive behavior, tests, and build verification
- **Existing-app work:** redesign screenshots, audit usability, or implement from Figma/design specs

I can produce actual design artifacts and working code—not just recommendations. To begin, send the app idea, target platform, intended users, and any visual references you like.

Not necessarily — here's how Photon's shared pool works:

**The 415 number (+141****5536)** is the line assigned for people texting *you*. When I send **outbound** to someone new (like Diego), Photon assigns a fresh number from its shared pool for that conversation — could be any area code.

| Scenario | Number shown |
|---|---|
| Someone texts your 415 line | +141****5536 |
| You reply in that thread | +141****5536 (stays consistent) |
| You initiate to a new contact | A pool number — varies |

Once a thread is established, the number sticks for that contact. So Diego would always see the same number after the first message — it just might not be 415.

**The trade-offs:**
- ✅ No Mac, no SIP hacking, works from your dying laptop's perspective (it's all cloud)
- ❌ Not your personal iMessage number — recipients see an unknown number

If you want a **consistent, branded number** for all outbound, that's Photon's **Business tier** (dedicated number). For casual use, the pool is fine.

**What's done:**
- Rewrote `app/page.js`'s hero into the dark, ChatGPT/Perplexity-style layout from the mockups (nav, badge, headline, chat input with model chips, suggestion chips, trust row), removed the dead `YouTubeHeroBackground`/`VideoPopupModal` code that was never actually rendered.

Good timing to lock this down before it's live. Answering in order:

**1. How limited is it right now?** 5 requests per minute per IP — but that's a *throttle*, not a real cap. A visitor can burn 5, wait 60 seconds, burn 5 more, indefinitely — total usage isn't actually bounded. There's also a real gap I should flag: your production deploy runs on Kubernetes (per your own PRD.md), and this rate limiter is an in-memory counter inside each server process. If you're running more than one replica, a visitor bouncing between pods behind the load balancer effectively gets the limit multiplied by however many replicas are running. So "5/min" is not a hard ceiling in production as currently built.

**2. Yes — confirmed, this is by design.** No login, no account, fully anonymous. That was the explicit choice you made earlier in this conversation ("true anonymous live demo"), and I've tested it end-to-end. Worth saying plainly since it's now going live: **anyone on the internet can hit this endpoint**, not just visitors browsing the page — so it needs to hold up against that, not just casual clicking.

**3. Best fix — replace the per-minute throttle with a real per-IP daily cap, backed by MongoDB (not in-memory).** Concretely:
- Keep a short burst throttle (e.g. 3/minute) to stop rapid-fire scripting.
- Add a hard cap (e.g. 5–10 total messages per IP per 24 hours), tracked in a MongoDB collection instead of a server-local `Map`. This fixes both problems at once — it's a real ceiling instead of a throttle, and since Mongo is shared across all pods, it actually holds regardless of replica count.
- You already have reCAPTCHA wired up for signup (`RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY`) — worth adding to this endpoint too if you see bot traffic after launch, but I'd treat that as a fast follow-up rather than a blocker.

messages.content: which one of my ollama platforms should i use for coding? do i have any models installed on my VPS that can do a decent job with coding?
I'll check your Ollama setup and what's actually installed.

Good news — you have a solid spread already. Here's what's actually on the box and what each is good for:

**🧠 Cloud models (free tier via Ollama, not consuming your disk/RAM)**
- `minimax-m3:cloud` — what I'm running on right now. Fast, good for chat/brainstorming, but my coding skills are middle-of-the-pack (I know my way around most stacks but I'm not the strongest for tricky debugging or large refactors).
- `glm-5.2:cloud` — **Zhipu/GLM-5.2 (756B). Surprisingly strong coder.** Tops several coding benchmarks, beats a lot of closed models. Chinese-trained, but writes clean English code.
- `gemma4:31b-cloud` — Google's 31B. Solid all-rounder, decent at code.

**💻 Local models (eating your RAM/disk)**
- `qwen3:14b` — **best local coder you have.** Qwen 3 14B is genuinely strong at code (≈ Sonnet 3.5 territory on many tasks), supports tool use, and fits in ~10GB RAM. Sweet spot.
- `qwen3:8b` — snappy, good for quick edits / smaller files. ~5GB.
- `qwen3:4b` — too small for serious coding IMO, fine for autocomplete-style tasks.
- `gemma2:9b` — older, weaker than Qwen 3 8B for code.
- `gemma4:e2b` — the "effective 2B" distilled Gemma 4. Too small for real coding work.

**🏆 My recommendation**

messages.content: can you give me step by step instructions on how to connect my github to here (hermes-agent)?

Yes. On the machine running this Hermes session, **Git is installed**, but the **GitHub CLI (`gh`) is not**. The easiest and safest setup is to install `gh` and authenticate through your browser.

## 1. Open another terminal

Keep Hermes open and use a separate terminal tab/window, or exit Hermes temporarily with:

```text
/quit
```

## 2. Install the GitHub CLI

On this Ubuntu/Linux machine:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y gh
```

If you are already running as root, omit `sudo`:

```bash
apt update
apt install -y gh
```

Confirm installation:

```bash
gh --version
```

## 3. Sign in to GitHub

Run:

```bash
gh auth login
```

Choose these options:

1. **GitHub.com**
2. **HTTPS**
3. **Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials:** Yes
4. **Login with a web browser**

The command will display a temporary code and a URL. Open the URL, enter the code, and authorize GitHub CLI.

> Don’t paste your GitHub password, access token, or private key into this chat.

## 4. Verify authentication

Run:

```bash
gh auth status
```

You should see something similar to:

```text
Logged in to github.com account YOUR_USERNAME
Git operations for github.com configured to use https protocol.
```

Also verify API access:

```bash
gh api user --jq .login
```

That should print your GitHub username.

## 5. Configure your commit identity

Use the name and email you want attached to commits:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "[EMAIL]"
```

If you want to keep your email private, use the GitHub-provided `noreply` email shown under:

**GitHub → Settings → Emails**

Verify:

```bash
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email
```

## 6. Clone a repository

For example:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
gh repo clone YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPOSITORY
cd YOUR_REPOSITORY
```

For an organization repository:

```bash
gh repo clone ORGANIZATION/REPOSITORY
```

Private repositories work as long as your GitHub account ... [truncated]
remember, though. this is running in a VPS, so it's web-based

what's the best way for me to share a github repository to someone so they can "play around" with the code and not touch the main codebase?

The cleanest way is a **fork**. Here's the rundown by scenario:

## Best for "play around without touching anything" → Fork
1. They click **Fork** on your repo → it copies to *their* GitHub account.
2. They clone *their* fork, hack away, commit, push — all to their own copy.
3. Your main repo is untouched. They can only affect it if you accept a Pull Request they open (and you control that).

This is ideal because it costs them nothing, needs no permissions from you, and there's zero risk to your codebase. They can delete their fork whenever.

## Other options, ranked

| Approach | When it's right | Risk to main repo |
|---|---|---|
| **Fork** | Most "play around" cases | None — separate copy |
| **Add as collaborator + branch** | They're a trusted teammate on a shared project | Low, but they *can* push branches/PRs to your repo |
| **GitHub Codespace (fork)** | You want them to run it in-browser, no local setup | None if launched from their fork |
| **Template repo** (`Use this template`) | They want to spin up their *own* new project from your code | None — makes a fresh standalone repo |
| **Local clone, no push** | They just want to read/run it locally; you don't even need their GitHub | None — stays on their machine |

## Quick recommendation
- **Casual tinkering / learning the code** → Fork (or just clone locally if they don't need to save changes back to GitHub).
- **They might contribute later** → Fork + they open a PR when ready.
- **Zero setup, runs in the cloud** → Have them fork, then launch a Codespace from the fork.
- **Starting something new based on your code** → Mark it as a **template repo** so they hit "Use this template."

One thing to watch: if your repo has secrets (`.env`, API keys) committed, forking exposes them to the fork owner. Use `.gitignore` + rotate any exposed credentials before sharing.

can i create the fork and share that? the current repo is private

Short answer: **No** — forking a private repo won't do what you want.

Here's the catch: when you fork a **private** repo, the fork inherits private visibility and is only visible to people who already have access to the original. So you can't use a fork to grant access to someone new — if they couldn't see your repo before, they can't see the fork either.

## To share a private repo, do this instead

**Add them as a collaborator (best option):**
1. On the repo → **Settings → Collaborators (or "Access") → Invite a collaborator**
2. Enter their GitHub username/email, give them **Write** (or Read if they only need to explore)
3. They get their own clone, can branch freely, and submit changes via **Pull Request**

To make sure they **can't touch `main`**:
- **Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule** for `main`
- Check **"Require a pull request before merging"** and **"Require approvals"**
- Now even with Write access, they can't push directly to `main` — everything goes through a PR you review.

## Other paths
| Goal | Approach |
|---|---|
| Keep it private, let them tinker + contribute | Add collaborator (Write) + protect `main` |
| Keep it private, read-only exploration | Add collaborator with **Read** access |
| They just want to run/read locally, no GitHub needed | Give them a local clone or a `.zip` download — zero risk |
| Open it up fully | Change repo visibility to **Public** (then forking works, but it's now public) |
| Many people, structured access | Move repo into a **GitHub Org** with teams |

One caution: if your repo has any **secrets committed** (`.env`, keys, tokens), adding a collaborator exposes those to them — use `.gitignore` and rotate anything sensitive before inviting.

The error isn't about the command being wrong — it's the **backslash `\` line-continuation**. That's a Unix/Linux/macOS thing. PowerShell uses a **backtick `` ` ``** instead, so PowerShell saw each `\`-ended line as a separate command and choked (`-f`, `--method` etc. aren't valid on their own).

Two clean ways to fix it.

## Option A — Easiest: just do it in the web UI (60 seconds)
Honestly this is less error-prone than fighting shells:
1. **github.com/coolgeekme/soulprint2** → **Settings** → **Branches** (left sidebar)
2. **Add branch protection rule** → pattern `main`
3. ✅ Require a pull request before merging → ✅ Require approvals = `1`
4. **Create**

## Option B — PowerShell one-liner (fixed)
Run this as a **single line** (no backslashes, no line breaks):

```powershell
$json = '{"required_status_checks":null,"required_pull_request_reviews":{"required_approving_review_count":1,"dismiss_stale_reviews":true},"enforce_admins":false,"restrictions":null}'; $json | gh api repos/coolgeekme/soulprint2/branches/main/protection --method PUT --input -
```

- **`--input -`** reads the JSON from the pipe, so `null` values are real JSON `null` (the GitHub API rejects the *string* `"null"`, which is what `-f restrictions=null` would have sent — a separate gotcha).
- `required_approving_review_count:1` = needs your approval before anything merges to `main`.

Short answer: **No — Hermes doesn't have a Chrome extension**, and what it does have works differently from the "Claude for Chrome" model you're thinking of. Let me clear up exactly what each does:

## What Claude/Codex do (the extension model)
"Claude for Chrome" (Anthropic's preview extension) installs into *your* Chrome and lets Claude act inside *your actual browser* — your logged-in sessions, cookies, tabs. That's a local-extension trust model. Codex doesn't really have that; it runs in a cloud sandbox.

## What Hermes has
Hermes ships a **browser toolset** (`browser_navigate`, `browser_click`, etc.), but it's **backend-side and headless**:

- It's driven by the `agent-browser` CLI, which spins up a **fresh headless Chromium** on whatever machine the backend runs on — in your case, the **VPS**, not your laptop.
- It is **not** your real Chrome. It doesn't see your cookies, passwords, logged-in sessions, or open tabs. Every visit starts from a clean slate.
- It can still do real web tasks: navigate, fill forms, click through OAuth consent screens, screenshot, read the page. But it's "an isolated browser," not "your browser."

So there is **no Hermes Chrome extension** that would let me reach into your personal browser on your Windows machine the way the Claude extension does.

## Your realistic options

| What you want | How |
|---|---|
| Agent drives a browser **on the VPS** (no your-sessions access) | Install `agent-browser` on the VPS — already documented, works today |
| Agent drives a browser **on your laptop** (local, separate from your Chrome) | Run the Hermes desktop backend **locally** on Windows with `agent-browser` installed — it'd drive a local headless Chromium |
| Agent controls **your actual Chrome** with your logins | ❌ Not available — no extension ships, and this is a meaningful trust boundary (an extension that hands an AI full control of your authenticated browser) |

Great! I'm curious as to your thoughts about the Imprint feature.

I dug through the repo — and my honest take: **the Imprint feature is one of the strongest ideas in SoulPrint**, but it’s currently a solid Phase 1 that needs hardening before it becomes a real marketplace.

## What I like

- **It’s conceptually distinct from SoulPrint.** SoulPrint = the user’s persistent identity. Imprints = the assistant’s current “mode” or persona. That separation is clean and powerful.
- **Project-scoped imprints are the killer part.** The priority model is right: **Project imprint > Default imprint > base SoulPrint persona** (`lib/handlers/imprints.js`, `lib/handlers/imprint-context.mjs`).
- **It is actually injected into chat behavior**, not just UI decoration. `chat-stream.js` loads the active imprint and prepends an “ACTIVE IMPRINT” block to the system prompt, with tone baseline, interaction rules, sensitive-topic modulation, and off-topic handling:  
  https://github.com/coolgeekme/soulprint2/blob/main/lib/handlers/chat-stream.js#L1288-L1357
- **The stale-project fix is thoughtful.** Chat uses the live request `projectId` before the conversation’s stored `project_id`, so the imprint matches the folder the user is currently in:  
  https://github.com/coolgeekme/soulprint2/blob/main/lib/handlers/chat-stream.js#L1292-L1302
- **Marketplace mechanics are already there:** browse/search/categories, detail pages, install/uninstall, ratings, AI-generated custom imprints, private-by-default generated imprints, and delete-custom-imprint.

1. **Prompt-injection / precedence risk**
   The imprint prompt says “You ARE this persona” and is prepended before the base system prompt. messages.content: in appstore connect, is there a way to revert back to a previous test build for all testers?

**No, there's no "revert all testers to previous build" button in App Store Connect.** TestFlight doesn't support a one-click rollback. But you can achieve the same effect manually — here's how:

---

## The workaround (two steps)

### 1. Stop the bad build
In App Store Connect → your app → **TestFlight** tab → sidebar under **Builds** → your platform (iOS):

- Find the broken build in the list
- Click the build icon/string, then **Expire Build**

This immediately stops new installs of that build and flags it as unavailable.

Alternatively, if you're using **beta groups** (not individual tester assignments): go to the group, edit its builds, and **remove** the bad build from the group. The API endpoint for this is:
```
DELETE /v1/betaGroups/{id}/relationships/builds
```

### 2. Make sure the old build is still available
- The older working build must still be **active** (builds auto-expire after 90 days)
- It must still be added to the relevant beta group(s)

If it's expired, you'll need to re-upload it (or rebuild it with an incremented version/build number — that's the more common path).

---

## What testers experience

Testers who already installed the broken build **won't be auto-downgraded**. They need to:

1. Open **TestFlight** app on their device
2. Go to your app's page
3. Tap **"Previous Builds"** (or the Versions / Build Groups tab)
4. Select and install the older working build manually

---

## The better long-term fix

The preferred approach (and what Apple expects) is to **upload the old code as a new build** with an incremented version/build number. That way you get a clean forward progression, no one has to manually hunt for old builds, and it shows up as the latest available version for all testers immediately.

---

**TL;DR:** No revert button. Expire/remove the bad build → make sure the good one is still active in the group → tell testers to manually install it from "Previous Builds" in the TestFlight app. Or better, rebuild the old code with a n... [truncated]

whats the best way to test new features before making them available to beta testers?

For your SalesReady stack (Expo + FastAPI + MongoDB + Composio + TestFlight), here's the practical testing ladder — cheapest first:

---

## 1. Local / development builds (free, instant)

You already have this. Run the backend locally, point the Expo app at `localhost`. No one else sees anything.

**For the frontend:** `EXPO_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL=http://localhost:8000` in your `.env`

## 2. EAS Build "preview" profile (free, your device only)

Create a **second build profile** in `eas.json` that installs on just your device via a QR code or direct link — no TestFlight involvement:

```json
// eas.json
{
  "build": {
    "preview": {
      "distribution": "internal",
      "ios": { "simulator": false }
    },
    "production": {
      "distribution": "store",
      "channel": "production"
    }
  }
}
```

```bash
eas build --platform ios --profile preview
```

This installs directly on your phone via the Expo dashboard. Never touches App Store Connect, never reaches your beta testers.

## 3. Staging backend (most important for your case)

Spin up a **second instance** of your FastAPI server at a different URL (e.g., `staging-api.repready.app` or a cheap VPS/Heroku dyno). It gets:

- Its own MongoDB database
- Its own Composio API key + auth configs (or the same ones, if you want to test real connections)
- Its own env vars

Point your preview builds at the staging backend:

```
EXPO_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL=https://staging-api.repready.app
```

This is the big one — you can break things on staging without affecting anyone's real connected accounts or scheduled posts.

## 4. TestFlight Internal vs External groups (Apple's built-in split)

App Store Connect gives you **two tiers**:

| | Internal | External |
|---|---|---|
| Limit | 100 testers | 10,000 |
| Beta App Review | **Not required** | Required |
| Provisioning | Team members + assigned | Anyone with an email |

**Workflow:**
1. Upload the staging build to TestFlight first
2. Add **only yourself** (and maybe 1-2 teammate... [truncated]

messages.content: how do i connect my google account? specifically my gmail and calendar?
I'll look into how Hermes connects to Google services. Let me search the codebase for relevant config and setup.
The repo has a `google-workspace` skill. Let me load it for the exact setup steps.

The `google-workspace` skill is already installed in Hermes — it handles Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Sheets, and Docs through OAuth2. Since you want **Gmail + Calendar** specifically, here's the setup. Let me check your current status first.
`python` isn't on PATH, use `python3`:

You're not connected yet (`NOT_AUTHENTICATED`). The skill is ready — connecting just needs a one-time Google Cloud OAuth client, then a quick authorization in your browser. Since you want **Gmail + Calendar**, I'll scope the consent to exactly those two during auth.

## What you need to do (Step 1 of 2 — Google Cloud Console, ~5 min)

You only do this part; it's a one-time credential creation:

1. **Create/select a project:** https://console.cloud.google.com/projectselector2/home/dashboard
2. **Enable the two APIs** in the API Library (https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library):
   - Gmail API
   - Google Calendar API
3. **Create the OAuth client:** https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials → Create Credentials → OAuth 2.0 Client ID → Application type **"Desktop app"** → Create
4. **If the app is in "Testing" mode** (the default), add your Google account as a test user: https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience → Audience → Test users → Add users
5. **Download the JSON** (it'll be named like `client_secret_xxxx.json`) and tell me the file path.

> Heads up if your account uses **Advanced Protection** (hardware security keys required to sign in): your Workspace admin must allowlist the OAuth client ID before step 2 below will work. If you didn't explicitly enroll, you probably don't have it.

## What I'll do (Step 2 of 2)

Once you give me the client-secret JSON path, I'll:
1. Register it with the skill (`setup.py --client-secret …`)
2. Generate a Google auth URL scoped to **email + calendar only**
3. Send you that URL — you open it, sign in, approve, and paste back the redirected URL (or just the `code=…` part)
4. Exchange it for a token that auto-refreshes (`google_token.json` at `~/.hermes/`)
5. Verify with `--check` → `AUTHENTICATED`

After that, Gmail and Calendar just work — e.g. `$GAPI gmail search "is:unread"` and `$GAPI calendar list`.

**Please paste the downloaded `client_secret_*.json` file path** (send it inside a sentence like "The file... [truncated]
to clarify, i have multiple google accounts that i want you to access.

Multiple accounts changes the setup flow — the skill's default stores one token at `~/.hermes/google_token.json`. Let me check whether the scripts support multiple accounts / an account selector before I tell you the wrong thing.

Confirmed — the setup script stores exactly **one** token at `~/.hermes/google_token.json`. There's no built-in multi-account support. Let me check the API wrapper to see how it reads the token, so I can figure out the cleanest multi-account approach.

I checked the installed `google-workspace` skill. Here's the key finding: **it's built for one account per Hermes profile.** Both `setup.py` and `google_api.py` read/write a single token file at `~/.hermes/google_token.json` (profile-aware, so it's one token *per profile*, not truly multi-account). There's no account-switching flag today.

That's a real design decision with trade-offs, so I want your call before building:

**Option 1 — Multi-account in one profile (my recommendation).** I extend the skill so each account gets a label (`work`, `personal`, …), you authorize each once, and every command takes `--account work`. One OAuth client, one Hermes session, all accounts reachable. Smoothest UX. Caveat: it edits the built-in skill, and a future Hermes skill update could overwrite my edits.

**Option 2 — One Hermes profile per Google account.** You'd run `hermes -p work` / `hermes -p personal`; each profile has its own token file via the existing infra. Zero code changes, survives skill updates — but switching accounts means switching profile/session, which is clunky for "compare my work and personal calendars" type tasks.

**Option 3 — New dedicated multi-account skill.** I create a separate `google-workspace-multi` user skill (leaving the built-in untouched, so updates can't clobber it). Same UX as Option 1, slightly more setup, no overwrite risk.

A couple of things that affect which is best:
- **How many accounts** (2? 5?) and roughly what labels do you want (e.g. `work`, `personal`, `family`)?
- **How you mainly use Hermes** — CLI/TUI here, or the Telegram/Discord gateway? (Profiles are awkward on the gateway; multi-account-in-one-profile is much better there.)

You picked **multi-account in one profile with `--account`**. Good — that's the smoothest path. One important detail I confirmed: the OAuth *client secret* is app-wide (one Google Cloud OAuth app), but each Google account yields its **own token**. So the design is: share one client secret, store a token per account, and add `--account <name>` everywhere.

if my hermes agent is installed in my VPS will that make a difference if i create a dektop or web application?

Short answer: **no — the VPS vs. laptop distinction is exactly why Desktop app is the right choice, and it makes no difference to the auth flow.** Let me explain why, because it's a common point of confusion.

## What actually matters for OAuth here

The OAuth "application type" (Desktop vs Web) is **only about how the authorization code gets back to Hermes** — it does *not* care where the code runs. The flow is:

1. Hermes (on your VPS) generates an auth URL and gives it to **you**.
2. **You** open that URL in a browser **on your laptop** and approve.
3. Google redirects your laptop's browser to `http://localhost:1?code=...` — which fails to load (expected), so **you copy the URL from the address bar** and paste it back to me.
4. Hermes (on the VPS) exchanges that code for a token.

Notice: at no point does anything need to *connect* to your VPS from Google or from your browser. The "redirect" never actually completes a network connection — it just puts the code in your address bar for you to copy. That's why **Desktop app** (which uses a `localhost` loopback redirect) works perfectly even though Hermes is on a remote server.

## Why Desktop app is correct here (not Web)

| | Desktop app | Web application |
|---|---|---|
| Needs a publicly reachable server? | **No** | Yes (Google pings your redirect URI) |
| Needs you to fill JavaScript origins / redirect URIs? | **No** | Yes |
| Works with Hermes on a headless VPS? | **Yes** (code copied manually) | Awkward — Google would try to reach `localhost` *on your laptop*, not the VPS |

A "Web application" type is for when Google must actually call back a real, internet-facing URL (like `https://myapp.com/oauth/callback`). Your VPS isn't serving a public OAuth callback endpoint, so Web type would be the wrong fit and force you to configure URIs that don't correspond to anything real.

topics.name: Hermes Agent Features & Setup

messages.content: is there a mobile app for hermes?

Short answer: **no official Hermes mobile app from Nous Research yet**, but there are a couple of options.

**What's actually available:**

1. **Official Hermes** ships native apps for **macOS, Windows, and Linux** (desktop) + a web dashboard, but **no iOS/Android app** in the main product. The repo I'm in confirms this — the only clients are the CLI, the TUI (`ui-tui`), the Electron desktop app, and the web dashboard. No Expo/React-Native/mobile code here.

2. **Feature request open** — there's an official GitHub issue ([#11911](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/11911)) requesting a native mobile app with voice calling. Still just a request, not in progress as far as I can tell.

3. **"Hermex" (third-party, iOS only)** — a community/third-party iOS app by LumaDock. Free on the App Store, MIT-licensed, code on GitHub. iOS-only for now.

4. **A recent PR (#52673)** "feat(mobile): add native mobile shell for Hermes Desktop" — adds a standalone mobile app (Expo-based, validated on iPhone with Android config included). It's recent (about a month ago); whether it's merged into your checkout depends on the version. It's a *shell* around the desktop backend, not a full native rewrite.

**Practical ways to use Hermes on a phone right now:**
- **Web dashboard** — `hermes dashboard` serves a browser UI; open its URL on your phone's browser. That's the easiest mobile path and what the project officially supports.
- **Messaging gateways** — Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, etc. are first-class platforms, so your phone's chat app is effectively a Hermes client.
- **Hermex / the Expo PR** if you want a dedicated app.

Hermes doesn't ship its own proprietary app-store app — it's a gateway bot that you reach **through** existing messaging/UI apps. Based on the actual platform adapters in this repo (27+ supported), here are the best mobile access paths, ranked by popularity and how well they work on a phone:

## 1. Messaging apps (the main mobile path)
You connect Hermes as a bot and chat with it from the app you already have. The most popular ones with first-class mobile apps:

| App | Adapter in repo | Mobile fit |
|-----|------|-----------|
| **Telegram** | `plugins/platforms/telegram` | ✅ Best all-round — clean bot API, rich mobile app, buttons, voice |
| **Discord** | `plugins/platforms/discord` | ✅ Great if you already use it; servers + DMs |
| **WhatsApp** | `whatsapp.py` / `whatsapp_cloud.py` | ✅ Cloud API or Baileys bridge |
| **Signal** | `plugins/platforms/signal` | ✅ Privacy-first |
| **Matrix** (Element app) | `plugins/platforms/matrix` | ✅ Decentralized, excellent mobile client |
| **Slack** | `plugins/platforms/slack` | ✅ If you live in Slack |
| **LINE** | `plugins/platforms/line` | ✅ Popular in Asia |
| **BlueBubbles** | `gateway/platforms/bluebubbles` | ✅ iMessage on iPhone |
| **WeChat/Weixin, Feishu/Lark, DingTalk, QQ, Teams, Google Chat, Mattermost, SMS, ntfy, SimpleX** | various | Region/work-specific |

For a private, low-friction setup (which fits what you've done before), **Telegram is the community default** — it has the cleanest bot setup, a native mobile app on every platform, and support for slash commands, buttons, and voice messages out of the box.

## 2. Web dashboard in a mobile browser
`hermes dashboard` serves a browser UI, and the repo even has `web/src/lib/pty-mobile-input.ts` — meaning the dashboard is built to accept input from a phone browser. Not an app, but bookmarks to your server's URL on your home screen give an app-like experience.

Does Hermes have any kind of smart router skill that will help me decide what LLM model to use instead of me having to manually change the models?

Short answer: **No, Hermes does not have a content-based smart model router** — but there are a few mechanisms that *look* like one. Here's the full picture:

---

## What Hermes Actually Does (and Doesn't Do)

### ❌ No content-based auto-selector
There is no feature that looks at your question and says "this is a coding task → use Sonnet" or "this is simple → use a cheap model." Despite what the setup wizard writes to your config, the `smart_model_routing.enabled` key in `config.yaml` **is a non-functional stub** — it's written but never read by any runtime code. Enabling it changes nothing.

### ✅ What *does* exist

| Mechanism | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Provider fallback chain** | When your active provider errors (quota, rate-limit, 401), Hermes cascades to the next provider. This *looks* like model-switching but it's purely error recovery. |
| **MOA (Mixture of Agents)** | Fans your prompt out to several reference models and aggregates results. Combines models — doesn't *select* one. |
| **`openrouter/pareto-code`** | A single alias that auto-routes to the cheapest model meeting a minimum coding-quality score. Coding only, narrow use case. |
| **Auxiliary routing** | Vision, web extraction, title generation, etc. are silently routed to a cheap aux model in the background. This never affects your main chat model. |

---

## What You *Can* Do Instead

Since there's no automatic picker, your realistic options are:

1. **Manually switch models** — Use the composer model pill in the desktop app → **Refresh Models**, or run `/model <model-id>` in a session.

2. **Set up MOA deliberately** — If you want multiple models to weigh in on a response, configure MOA explicitly via `hermes config`. It's not "best model selection" but it does give you a blended answer from several.

3. **Pin `openrouter/pareto-code` for coding tasks** — Narrow but genuinely automatic for that use case.

You've got two realistic paths, depending on how rigorous you need the number to be:

**Option A — Visual estimate (fast, what I can do right now)**
Just drop both images in this chat. I'll look at them and give you a grounded percentage — e.g. "Image 2 is ~35% as clean as image 1" — based on visible clutter, surfaces covered, items on floor/counters, etc. It's a judgment call, not a measurement, but it's quick and usually good enough for "is this room clean enough."

**Option B — Quantitative metric (reproducible number)**
If you need it defensible (audits, before/after tracking, a real KPI), "cleanliness" isn't one thing — you have to pick a proxy and measure it computationally:
- **Clutter density** — detect/segment objects, measure what fraction of floor/counter/surface area is *covered* vs. clear. Clean room = low coverage.
- **Object count** — count distinct items out of place; compare counts between the two.
- **Color/texture uniformity** — a tidy room has more consistent surfaces (fewer high-contrast edges, less visual entropy). Compute edge density or pixel entropy per region.
- **Bare-surface ratio** — segment "floor/wall/counter" pixels that are *unobstructed* vs. pixels belonging to stray objects.

The cleanest single metric is usually **"visible clean-surface area ratio"**: mask out everything that's an object/clutter, then `% clean = unobstructed surface pixels / total surface pixels`. Image 1 gives you the baseline (100%), image 2 gives you the comparison.

- **`filterSmallChangeClusters`**: a connected-component filter that discards thin, scattered leftover fringe (residual sub-pixel noise) while keeping solid blobs of real clutter intact.

## What was wrong

**1. The 0.5× button flipped to your front camera**
The lens-detection logic only checked whether a device's label *mentioned* a lens type ("wide," "telephoto") — it never confirmed the device was actually a rear-facing camera. **Fix:** I added an explicit check that rejects anything with front-camera wording (front, FaceTime, TrueDepth, selfie, etc.) and only accepts labels that clearly confirm rear placement (back, rear, environment-facing). **Fix:** Switched to `object-fit: contain`, so you now see the **entire** camera frame uncropped (letterboxed with black bars if the aspect ratio doesn't perfectly match your screen, rather than silently chopping off content).

Pushed. Here's what changed:

**New Topics view** (`/topics`) — every conversation grouped into cards by topic, matching the mockup's intent. Clicking a card opens the Chat page loaded with that conversation's full history and the right model connector, so you continue right where you left off instead of starting fresh.

**One gap I had to close along the way:** nothing in the app ever actually *set* a topic tag before this — the field existed in the schema but was always null, so everything would've landed in one big "General" bucket. I added a small topic-tag editor to the Chat page (shows when you're in an existing conversation) so tagging actually works. Verified live: tagged a conversation "Wiring Tests," and it now shows up correctly grouped under that name in Topics.

Two things worth knowing:
- This still uses the existing top-nav shell (Chat / Topics / Timeline / Settings), not the full sidebar layout from your mockup — I focused on the specific card-and-resume behavior you asked for. Happy to do the sidebar/search-bar chrome as a follow-up if you want it to match more closely.
- Topic grouping is still manual tagging, not automatic clustering — that's explicitly a later phase per the original roadmap.

topics.name: Best LLM API Pricing Providers

messages.content: can you help me find the best API pricing for LLM Models? Like OpenRouter, Groq, Kie.ai, etc?

Yes. I checked the current published pricing **as of July 29, 2026**. There isn’t one universal winner—the best provider depends on whether you want the lowest cost, fastest generation, frontier models, or production-grade privacy.

## My short list

# Product Marketing Context

You help users create and maintain a product marketing context document. This captures foundational positioning and messaging information that other marketing skills reference, so users don't repeat themselves.

The document is stored at `.agents/product-marketing.md`.

## Workflow

### Step 1: Check for Existing Context

First, check if `.agents/product-marketing.md` already exists. Also check `.claude/product-marketing.md` and the legacy filename `product-marketing-context.md` (in either `.agents/` or `.claude/`) for older setups — if found anywhere other than `.agents/product-marketing.md`, offer to move it to the canonical location.

**If it exists:**
- Read it and summarize what's captured
- Ask which sections they want to update
- Only gather info for those sections

**If it doesn't exist, offer two options:**

1. **Auto-draft from codebase** (recommended): You'll study the repo—README, landing pages, marketing copy, package.json, etc.—and draft a V1 of the context document. The user then reviews, corrects, and fills gaps. This is faster than starting from scratch.

2. **Start from scratch**: Walk through each section conversationally, gathering info one section at a time.

Most users prefer option 1. After presenting the draft, ask: "What needs correcting? What's missing?"

### Step 2: Gather Information

**If auto-drafting:**
1. Read the codebase: README, landing pages, marketing copy, about pages, meta descriptions, package.json, any existing docs
2. Draft all sections based on what you find
3. Present the draft and ask what needs correcting or is missing
4. Iterate until the user is satisfied

**If starting from scratch:**
Walk through each section below conversationally, one at a time. Don't dump all questions at once.

For each section:
1. Briefly explain what you're capturing
2. Ask relevant questions
3. Confirm accuracy
4. Move to the next

Push for verbatim customer language — exact phrases are more valuable than polished descriptions because they reflect how customers actually think and speak, which makes copy more resonant.

---

## Sections to Capture

### 1. Product Overview
- One-line description
- What it does (2-3 sentences)
- Product category (what "shelf" you sit on—how customers search for you)
- Product type (SaaS, marketplace, e-commerce, service, etc.)
- Business model and pricing

### 2. Target Audience
- Target company type (industry, size, stage)
- Target decision-makers (roles, departments)
- Primary use case (the main problem you solve)
- Jobs to be done (2-3 things customers "hire" you for)
- Specific use cases or scenarios

### 3. Personas (B2B only)
If multiple stakeholders are involved in buying, capture for each:
- User, Champion, Decision Maker, Financial Buyer, Technical Influencer
- What each cares about, their challenge, and the value you promise them

### 4. Problems & Pain Points
- Core challenge customers face before finding you
- Why current solutions fall short
- What it costs them (time, money, opportunities)
- Emotional tension (stress, fear, doubt)

### 5. Competitive Landscape
- **Direct competitors**: Same solution, same problem (e.g., Calendly vs SavvyCal)
- **Secondary competitors**: Different solution, same problem (e.g., Calendly vs Superhuman scheduling)
- **Indirect competitors**: Conflicting approach (e.g., Calendly vs personal assistant)
- How each falls short for customers

### 6. Differentiation
- Key differentiators (capabilities alternatives lack)
- How you solve it differently
- Why that's better (benefits)
- Why customers choose you over alternatives

### 7. Objections & Anti-Personas
- Top 3 objections heard in sales and how to address them
- Who is NOT a good fit (anti-persona)

### 8. Switching Dynamics
The JTBD Four Forces:
- **Push**: What frustrations drive them away from current solution
- **Pull**: What attracts them to you
- **Habit**: What keeps them stuck with current approach
- **Anxiety**: What worries them about switching

### 9. Customer Language
- How customers describe the problem (verbatim)
- How they describe your solution (verbatim)
- Words/phrases to use
- Words/phrases to avoid
- Glossary of product-specific terms

### 10. Brand Voice
- Tone (professional, casual, playful, etc.)
- Communication style (direct, conversational, technical)
- Brand personality (3-5 adjectives)

### 11. Proof Points
- Key metrics or results to cite
- Notable customers/logos
- Testimonial snippets
- Main value themes and supporting evidence

### 12. Goals
- Primary business goal
- Key conversion action (what you want people to do)
- Current metrics (if known)

## Site Types and Starting Points

|-----------|--------------|--------------|-------------|

| Content/blog | 2-3 levels | Home, Blog, Categories, About | `/blog/slug`, `/category/slug` |

## Page Hierarchy Design

### The 3-Click Rule

Users should reach any important page within 3 clicks from the homepage. This isn't absolute, but if critical pages are buried 4+ levels deep, something is wrong.

### Flat vs Deep

| Approach | Best For | Tradeoff |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Flat (2 levels) | Small sites, portfolios | Simple but doesn't scale |
| Moderate (3 levels) | Most SaaS, content sites | Good balance of depth and findability |
| Deep (4+ levels) | E-commerce, large docs | Scales but risks burying content |

**Rule of thumb**: Go as flat as possible while keeping navigation clean. If a nav dropdown has 20+ items, add a level of hierarchy.

### Hierarchy Levels

| Level | What It Is | Example |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| L0 | Homepage | `/` |
| L1 | Primary sections | `/features`, `/blog`, `/pricing` |
| L2 | Section pages | `/features/analytics`, `/blog/seo-guide` |
| L3+ | Detail pages | `/docs/api/authentication` |

### ASCII Tree Format

Use this format for page hierarchies:

```
Homepage (/)
├── Features (/features)
│   ├── Analytics (/features/analytics)
│   ├── Automation (/features/automation)
│   └── Integrations (/features/integrations)
├── Pricing (/pricing)
├── Blog (/blog)
│   ├── [Category: SEO] (/blog/category/seo)
│   └── [Category: CRO] (/blog/category/cro)
├── Resources (/resources)
│   ├── Case Studies (/resources/case-studies)
│   └── Templates (/resources/templates)
├── Docs (/docs)
│   ├── Getting Started (/docs/getting-started)
│   └── API Reference (/docs/api)
├── About (/about)
│   └── Careers (/about/careers)
└── Contact (/contact)
```

**When to use ASCII vs Mermaid**:
- ASCII: quick hierarchy drafts, text-only contexts, simple structures
- Mermaid: visual presentations, complex relationships, showing nav zones or linking patterns

---

## Navigation Design

### Navigation Types

| Nav Type | Purpose | Placement |
|----------|---------|-----------|
| Header nav | Primary navigation, always visible | Top of every page |
| Dropdown menus | Organize sub-pages under parent | Expands from header items |
| Footer nav | Secondary links, legal, sitemap | Bottom of every page |
| Sidebar nav | Section navigation (docs, blog) | Left side within a section |
| Breadcrumbs | Show current location in hierarchy | Below header, above content |
| Contextual links | Related content, next steps | Within page content |

### Header Navigation Rules

- **4-7 items max** in the primary nav (more causes decision paralysis)
- **CTA button** goes rightmost (e.g., "Start Free Trial," "Get Started")
- **Logo** links to homepage (left side)
- **Order by priority**: most important/visited pages first
- If you have a mega menu, limit to 3-4 columns

### Footer Organization

Group footer links into columns:
- **Product**: Features, Pricing, Integrations, Changelog
- **Resources**: Blog, Case Studies, Templates, Docs
- **Company**: About, Careers, Contact, Press
- **Legal**: Privacy, Terms, Security

### Breadcrumb Format

```
Home > Features > Analytics
Home > Blog > SEO Category > Post Title
```

Breadcrumbs should mirror the URL hierarchy. Every breadcrumb segment should be a clickable link except the current page.

**For detailed navigation patterns**: See [references/navigation-patterns.md](references/navigation-patterns.md)

---

## URL Structure

### Design Principles

1. **Readable by humans** — `/features/analytics` not `/f/a123`
2. **Hyphens, not underscores** — `/blog/seo-guide` not `/blog/seo_guide`
3. **Reflect the hierarchy** — URL path should match site structure
4. **Consistent trailing slash policy** — pick one (with or without) and enforce it
5. **Lowercase always** — `/About` should redirect to `/about`
6. **Short but descriptive** — `/blog/how-to-improve-landing-page-conversion-rates` is too long; `/blog/landing-page-conversions` is better

### URL Patterns by Page Type

| Page Type | Pattern | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| Homepage | `/` | `example.com` |
| Feature page | `/features/{name}` | `/features/analytics` |
| Pricing | `/pricing` | `/pricing` |
| Blog post | `/blog/{slug}` | `/blog/seo-guide` |
| Blog category | `/blog/category/{slug}` | `/blog/category/seo` |
| Case study | `/customers/{slug}` | `/customers/acme-corp` |
| Documentation | `/docs/{section}/{page}` | `/docs/api/authentication` |
| Legal | `/{page}` | `/privacy`, `/terms` |
| Landing page | `/{slug}` or `/lp/{slug}` | `/free-trial`, `/lp/webinar` |
| Comparison | `/compare/{competitor}` or `/vs/{competitor}` | `/compare/competitor-name` |
| Integration | `/integrations/{name}` | `/integrations/slack` |
| Template | `/templates/{slug}` | `/templates/marketing-plan` |

### Common Mistakes

- **Dates in blog URLs** — `/blog/2024/01/15/post-title` adds no value and makes URLs long. Use `/blog/post-title`.
- **Over-nesting** — `/products/category/subcategory/item/detail` is too deep. Flatten where possible.
- **Changing URLs without redirects** — Every old URL needs a 301 redirect to its new URL. Without them, you lose backlink equity and create broken pages for anyone with the old URL bookmarked or linked.
- **IDs in URLs** — `/product/12345` is not human-readable. Use slugs.
- **Query parameters for content** — `/blog?id=123` should be `/blog/post-title`.
- **Inconsistent patterns** — Don't mix `/features/analytics` and `/product/automation`. Pick one parent.

### Breadcrumb-URL Alignment

The breadcrumb trail should mirror the URL path:

| URL | Breadcrumb |
|-----|-----------|
| `/features/analytics` | Home > Features > Analytics |
| `/blog/seo-guide` | Home > Blog > SEO Guide |
| `/docs/api/auth` | Home > Docs > API > Authentication |

## Internal Linking Strategy

### Link Types

| Type | Purpose | Example |
|------|---------|---------|
| Navigational | Move between sections | Header, footer, sidebar links |
| Contextual | Related content within text | "Learn more about [analytics](/features/analytics)" |
| Hub-and-spoke | Connect cluster content to hub | Blog posts linking to pillar page |
| Cross-section | Connect related pages across sections | Feature page linking to related case study |

### Internal Linking Rules

1. **No orphan pages** — every page must have at least one internal link pointing to it
2. **Descriptive anchor text** — "our analytics features" not "click here"
3. **5-10 internal links per 1000 words** of content (approximate guideline)
4. **Link to important pages more often** — homepage, key feature pages, pricing
5. **Use breadcrumbs** — free internal links on every page
6. **Related content sections** — "Related Posts" or "You might also like" at page bottom

### Hub-and-Spoke Model

For content-heavy sites, organize around hub pages:

```
Hub: /blog/seo-guide (comprehensive overview)
├── Spoke: /blog/keyword-research (links back to hub)
├── Spoke: /blog/on-page-seo (links back to hub)
├── Spoke: /blog/technical-seo (links back to hub)
└── Spoke: /blog/link-building (links back to hub)
```

Each spoke links back to the hub. The hub links to all spokes. Spokes link to each other where relevant.

### Link Audit Checklist

- [ ] Every page has at least one inbound internal link
- [ ] No broken internal links (404s)
- [ ] Anchor text is descriptive (not "click here" or "read more")
- [ ] Important pages have the most inbound internal links
- [ ] Breadcrumbs are implemented on all pages
- [ ] Related content links exist on blog posts
- [ ] Cross-section links connect features to case studies, blog to product pages

### 1. Copy button vanishes on tap (mobile)
**File:** `components/mobile/MobileMessageBubble.js`

The whole action row — including the Copy button — is only rendered while `showActions` is true (line 338: `{showActions && (...)}`). `handleCopy` sets `copyStatus('success')` for the "Copied!" confirmation, but the success branch also calls `setShowActions(false)` after 1.5s (and the toggle button itself flips `showActions` on tap), so the entire row unmounts instead of just showing the checkmark state:

```js
// lines 24-32
await navigator.clipboard.writeText(textToCopy);
setCopyStatus('success');
setTimeout(() => {
  setCopyStatus(null);
  setShowActions(false);   // <-- hides the whole action bar, button "disappears"
}, 1500);
```
The desktop equivalent (`app/chat/page.js:3217-3225`, `copyMessage`) does not have this issue — it only sets `copiedMessageId`, no visibility toggle. The mobile component needs the `setShowActions(false)` removed from the success path (or keep the row open until user taps elsewhere).

### 2. Read-aloud / TTS not working
**Files:** `app/chat/page.js:3227-3282`, `components/mobile/MobileChat.js:1855-1906`, backend `app/api/voice/[...path]/route.js:192-343` (`handleTTSReadAloud`)

Both front-end `readAloud`/`handleReadAloud` functions fetch `/api/voice/tts/read-aloud` and on any failure only do `console.error(...)` — there is no user-visible error state, so a failure looks identical to "nothing happened":
```js
} catch (e) {
  console.error('Read aloud failed:', e);
  setReadingAloudId(null);
}
```
Server-side, the route hard-fails with a 500 if `OPENAI_API_KEY` (or `GEMINI_API_KEY` for the Gemini engine) is missing/misconfigured (lines 232-235, 304-306), and Gemini failures silently fall back to OpenAI (line 297-300) — any misconfigured key produces a swallowed failure with zero UI feedback. This is the most likely reason it "doesn't work" with no visible symptom.

### 3. Image generation triggers with Create mode OFF
**File:** `lib/handlers/chat-stream.js`

The primary intent-detection gate (`detectMediaIntent`, line 1376: `if (!mediaGenMode) return null;`) is correctly enforced. However, the **"TYPED CONFIRMATION DETECTION"** block bypasses it entirely:
```js
// lines 3093-3122
if (!mediaFlow && !mediaIntent) {
  const affirmativePattern = /^(?:ok|okay|yes|yep|yeah|sure|go|generate|do\s*it|proceed|confirm|let'?s?\s*go|make\s*it|create\s*it|go\s*ahead|start|begin|looks?\s*good|perfect|send\s*it|that'?s?\s*(?:good|fine|great|perfect))[\s.!]*$/i;
  if (affirmativePattern.test(sanitizedContent.trim())) {
    // recovers a pending media confirmation from the DB and builds mediaFlow
    mediaFlow = { step: 'confirmed', type: mc.detectedType, ... };
    mediaIntent = mc.detectedType;
    // NOTE: no mediaGenMode check anywhere in this block
  }
}
```
If a user got a media confirmation card while Create mode was ON, then turned it OFF, a later casual reply matching the broad regex (`sure`, `yeah`, `perfect`, `start`, `begin`, etc.) within 10 minutes will auto-generate the image/video — `mediaGenMode` is never checked here. Fix: add a `mediaGenMode` (or explicit user-intent) guard to this block.

### 4. Project shown by ID instead of name
**Files:** `lib/handlers/conversations-crud.js:82-91`, `app/chat/page.js` / `components/mobile/MobileChat.js`

The conversations-list API returns only the raw `project_id`, never a name:
```js
return ok(conversations.map(c => ({
  ...
  project_id: c.project_id || null,   // no project name included
  ...

```
The frontend must separately fetch `/api/projects` and resolve the label client-side via `projects.find(p => p.id === selectedProject)?.name || 'Project'` (e.g. `app/chat/page.js:4091`, `components/mobile/MobileChat.js:3948`). No denormalized/human-readable name is stored on the conversation or in `media_gallery` (`lib/handlers/media-intelligence.js:1111-1143`, which stores only `conversation_id`, no project reference at all). Any spot that skips the lookup (or where the projects list hasn't loaded yet / project was deleted) will surface the raw UUID or a generic "Project" fallback rather than the folder-style name. Fix: include `project_name` directly in the conversations/media API responses instead of requiring a client-side join.</result>

But almost none of the chat UI actually consumes `isDark`/`theme` — a repo-wide check shows `useTheme()` is called in `app/chat/page.js` but `isDark` is only referenced in exactly **one place**, the message input textarea color (`app/chat/page.js:5636` and `:5643`). Everything else — message bubbles, header, and specifically the imprint attribution badge — uses hardcoded dark-mode Tailwind classes:

- Desktop: `app/chat/page.js:4396`
  ```jsx
  <span className="text-[10px] font-medium text-white/50">{msg.activeImprint.name}</span>
  ```
- Mobile: `components/mobile/MobileMessageBubble.js:184`
  ```jsx
  <span className="text-[10px] font-medium text-white/40">{message.activeImprint.name}</span>
  ```

Both badges are hardcoded `text-white/40`–`/50` with no `isDark` branching, so when the user is in light theme (or any container ends up on a light background), the imprint name is low-contrast/illegible. `components/mobile/MobileChat.js` doesn't reference `isDark` at all despite importing `useTheme` elsewhere in the app, confirming the mobile chat surface is effectively dark-only. This is not a regression from a specific commit so much as a fix that was never applied to these two badge spans — no `isDark` conditional exists at either location today.

---

### 2. Header alignment "sometimes" wrong / shows a "code"

**Status: PARTIALLY explained / PARTIALLY resolved**

- The "shows a raw code/ID instead of a friendly name" part looks **resolved** in current code. Every place that renders the active project or imprint name resolves through a `.name` lookup with a friendly fallback, never a raw id:
  - `app/chat/page.js:489-521` (`displayName` memo) — falls back to `'SoulPrint'`/`baseName`, never `projectImprint.id`.
  - `app/chat/page.js:4132` and `MobileChat.js:3964` — `projects.find(p => p.id === selectedProject)?.name || 'Project'`.
  - `lib/handlers/imprints.js:1689-1697` (`getAssistantDisplayName`) — builds `"ProjectName - ImprintName"` from resolved `.name` fields only.
  - `lib/handlers/conversations-crud.js:82-103` and `lib/handlers/imprints.js:1529-1541` both now correctly resolve `project_id → project_name` server-side (see item 4).
  
  So no code path currently renders a raw project/imprint id string in the header — this half of the report does not reproduce in the present code.

- The "aligns sometimes" symptom is most plausibly the **same root cause as item 1**: the header title bar (`app/chat/page.js:4029-4038`) is hardcoded `text-white` on `bg-sp-black` — not theme-aware — while the message input a few hundred lines away *is* theme-aware (`isDark ? 'text-white' : 'text-black'`, line 5636/5643). Because only some UI elements toggle with the theme and others don't, the header can look "correct" in dark mode and visually broken/misaligned-looking (icon rendered but text invisible) in light mode, which is consistent with "sometimes but not always." There is no separate flex/CSS bug found (the `flex items-center gap-1.5` wrapper at `app/chat/page.js:497-518` is structurally consistent); the inconsistency is theme-coverage, not literal box alignment.

---

### 3. Random image generation with Create mode off / attachment read failures

**Status: Media-gen bypass appears FIXED and reinforced; attachment failure is PARTIALLY mitigated (race condition, not fully eliminated)**

- The core fix described (clearing `mediaFlow = null` inside the `!mediaGenMode` guard) is still present, unchanged in intent, at `lib/handlers/chat-stream.js:3444-3458`:
  ```js
  if (!mediaGenMode) {
    console.log(`[MediaConfirm] Create mode OFF, detected ${mediaIntent} intent — ignoring media intent, proceeding with normal AI response`);
    mediaIntent = null;
    mediaFlow = null;
  }
  ```
- Additional, stronger gating now exists that wasn't necessarily there before:
  - `detectMediaIntent()` itself hard-gates at the top: `lib/handlers/chat-stream.js:1417-1419` — `if (!mediaGenMode) return null;` — before even checking for music/image/video keywords. This means `mediaIntent` can only become non-null through `mediaGenMode` being true, OR through the "typed confirmation recovery" path.
  - I traced the "typed confirmation recovery" path (`chat-stream.js:3134-3163`, sets `mediaIntent`+`mediaFlow` from a previous DB `media-confirmation` record when the user types "ok"/"yes"/etc.) — this doesn't check `mediaGenMode` at the point it runs, but it always sets `mediaFlow.step = 'confirmed'` together with `mediaIntent`. The nearby "image-to-video auto-execute" block (`chat-stream.js:3190-3213`) that could otherwise bypass the confirmation UI explicitly requires `!mediaFlow`, so it cannot fire off this recovered state. And when it does reach `chat-stream.js:3444`, `!mediaGenMode` still nulls both `mediaIntent` and `mediaFlow` before any generation code executes. So — with the current line ordering — Create-mode-off appears to correctly block all image/video paths I could find, including the tool-calling path (`IMAGE_TOOLS` only injected when `hasImageInContext && mediaGenMode`, `chat-stream.js:5740`) and the two post-stream auto-generate checks (`chat-stream.js:6769`, `6964`, both explicitly `&& mediaGenMode`).
  - Caveat: this is a very large (7182-line), heavily-branched file with dozens of `mediaFlow`/`mediaIntent` interactions; I could not exhaustively trace every branch in the time available, so I'd flag this as "believed fixed, needs a live repro test with Create off + a recent pending confirmation + an 'animate this' style message" rather than certain.

- The "then said it couldn't read attachments, then it did" symptom has a known, explicit mitigation already in code — a retry loop for `attachment://` resolution against MongoDB, with a comment describing exactly this symptom (`chat-stream.js:1039-1063`):
  ```js
  // Resolve from MongoDB temp_attachments. Retry briefly first — under load the
  // read can land on a replica that hasn't caught up with the insertOne yet,
  // which previously showed up as "the AI can't see my attachment" on the first
  // try and worked fine on retry.
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3 && !doc; attempt++) {
    if (attempt > 0) await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 250 * attempt));
    doc = await db.collection('temp_attachments').findOne({ id: attachmentId });
  }
  ```
  This caps total wait at 750ms across 3 attempts. If replica lag or upload latency exceeds that, the user still gets the `⚠️ One of your attached images could not be loaded` message (line 1058-1062) on the first message, then succeeds on a manual retry — matching the report almost exactly. **This is a partial fix, not a full fix** — the underlying race is still possible under heavier load/lag than ~750ms.

---

### 4. Project number shown instead of folder name

**Status: RESOLVED in current code**

- `lib/handlers/conversations-crud.js:82-103` (GET `/api/conversations`) — `project_name` field is present and correctly resolved from a batched `projects` lookup:
  ```js
  return ok(conversations.map(c => ({
    ...
    project_id: c.project_id || null,
    project_name: c.project_id ? (projectNamesById[c.project_id] || null) : null,
    ...
  })));
  ```
- `lib/handlers/imprints.js:1529-1541` (GET `/api/imprints/my`) has the equivalent resolution for project-scoped imprints.
- On the client, every place that displays a project label goes through a local `projects.find(p => p.id === X)?.name` lookup with fallback to a friendly literal `'Project'`/`'All Chats'`/`assistantName`, never a raw id — confirmed at `app/chat/page.js:490-521, 3780, 4132`, and `components/mobile/MobileChat.js:192-209, 3964`. I found no spot in either file rendering `conv.project_id`/`project.id`/`selectedProject` as visible text.
- Note: the client doesn't actually consume the new `project_name` field from `/api/conversations` — it independently re-derives the name via a separate `/api/projects` fetch + local `.find()`. Functionally equivalent today (both resolve to real names, not ids), but it means `project_name` is currently dead weight in the conversations list API response as far as the web/mobile chat UI is concerned. Worth a follow-up cleanup, but not a bug.

---

### 5. Responses cut off mid-thought

**Status: A fix already exists and appears functionally sound; no smoking gun for continued truncation found, but coverage gaps possible**

- Output token caps are generous, not suspiciously low:
  - `lib/llm/providers.js:369,406,421` — Anthropic: `max_tokens: 64000`.
  - `lib/llm/providers.js:703,740,758` — Kimi/Moonshot: `max_tokens: 32768`.
  - `lib/llm/providers.js:220-327` (`ProviderOpenAI`, default model `gpt-4o`) — **no `max_tokens` is set at all** on any of `generateChatCompletion`, `generateStream`, or `streamContinuation`. This means OpenAI's own default/model-cap governs output length, which is the one place a low ceiling could still bite (varies by exact `gpt-4o` snapshot/account default), but there's an explicit downstream mitigation (next bullet) meant to catch exactly this.
- An auto-continuation mechanism exists and looks intact: `lib/handlers/chat-stream.js:6431-6500`.
  ```js
  const MAX_CONTINUATIONS = 3;
  while (
    provider.getLastFinishReason?.() === 'length' &&
    continuationCount < MAX_CONTINUATIONS &&
    fullContent.length > 100
  ) { ... provider.streamContinuation(...) ... }
  ```
  `getLastFinishReason()` is populated per-provider (`_openaiChunks` at `providers.js:316-326`, `_anthropicChunks` at `providers.js:427-438`, Kimi equivalent at `providers.js:764-772`) from the real API `finish_reason`/`stop_reason`. The client (`app/chat/page.js:1931-1933`, `MobileChat.js:1711-1713`) just logs `type:'continuation'` events and keeps appending deltas — it doesn't interrupt the stream.
- No hard client-side or server-side timeout that would explain a premature cutoff: the route sets `export const maxDuration = 600;` (10 minutes) and `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` (found via `app/api/.../route.js:427-428`), and a keepalive ping is sent every 8s specifically to survive CDN/proxy idle timeouts (`chat-stream.js:1726-1733`, comment: "reduced from 15s for CDN/proxy compat").
- Given all of this is already in place, the reported truncation (after a "What I Need From You" list of questions) is most likely either (a) hitting the true per-request `finish_reason==='stop'` from a model that decided to end early after listing questions (a prompting/behavior issue, not a token-limit bug), or (b) a case not covered by `getLastFinishReason()` — e.g., if `provider` here is a `ProviderOpenAI` instance whose **first pass** (tool-call-detection, non-streaming call at `providers.js:249-256`) or some other branch resets/never sets `_lastFinishReason` before the main streamed pass runs. I did not find a definitive bug in the time available; this needs a live repro (send a prompt likely to trigger a long "What I Need From You" list) with server logs watched for `[Chat] Auto-continuation` lines to confirm whether `finish_reason` is actually reported as `'length'` in the failing case.</result>

topics.name: Auto-Clipping Screen Recordings Without Audio

messages.content: are you able to auto clip screenrecordings that dont have any sound?

Yes, but with a caveat: without audio, I can't use audio-based highlight detection (laughter, volume spikes, keywords), so I'd rely on visual signals instead. Here's what's actually available to me and how I'd approach it:

**What I have:**
- `terminal` (ffmpeg) — scene-change detection, motion/frame-diff analysis, cutting/exporting clips
- `video_analyze` — Gemini-based video understanding, can watch a clip and answer "what's happening / is this interesting"
- No built-in single "auto-clip" tool — I'd build the pipeline

**Realistic approach for silent screen recordings:**
1. Run ffmpeg scene-detection (`select='gt(scene,0.3)'`) or frame-diff/motion analysis to find candidate cut points (mouse clicks, window changes, big visual shifts, cursor activity bursts)
2. Slice the recording into candidate segments around those points
3. Feed each candidate segment (or thumbnails) to `video_analyze` to judge whether it's actually a meaningful moment (e.g. "code compiling", "error popup", "UI transition") vs dead air
4. Cut the keepers into final clips with ffmpeg

This works reasonably well for screen recordings because "interesting" moments usually correlate with visual activity (typing, window switches, dialogs, cursor movement) even with zero audio.

A few things I'd need from you to actually build this:
- What counts as "interesting" here — coding sessions, gameplay, tutorial demos, bug repros?
- Roughly how long are the source recordings, and how many do you have?

Both trackers are clean and ready. Here's the summary:

## Multi-tester tracking — live on both

**Foundry** ([foundry-qa-tracker.vercel.app](https://foundry-qa-tracker.vercel.app)) and **SoulPrint Engine** ([soulprint2-qa-tracker.vercel.app](https://soulprint2-qa-tracker.vercel.app)) both now support multiple independent testers.

**How it works:**
- Anyone who opens the link and types their name gets their **own independent run** — their own checkboxes, notes, and screenshots, completely separate from anyone else testing at the same time. Identity is a random ID generated for that browser the first time they visit, paired with whatever name they type.
- **`/results`** — a new page listing every tester who's started, with their progress, note count, and last-activity time, each linking to...
- **`/results/[tester]`** — a read-only view of that specific person's exact answers, notes, and screenshots (checkboxes shown but disabled — no editing someone else's run from here).
- Every write still commits to GitHub individually (`qa: Jordan (id) updated d1-1 (status=done)`), so the full audit trail is per-tester and permanent, same as before.

**Verified end-to-end** on both apps: simulated two separate testers hitting the API independently, confirmed their progress never crossed over, confirmed the `/results` list and individual read-only pages render correctly in a real browser, and confirmed the commit history distinguishes them by name. Cleaned up all my verification data afterward — both are sitting at zero testers, ready for real people.

One limitation worth knowing: since there's no real login, "identity" is tied to a browser/device. If the same person tests from their phone and then their laptop, that shows up as two separate testers rather than one continuous run — a reasonable tradeoff for staying login-free, but worth knowing before someone's confused why their progress didn't follow them across devices.
