sessions.title: Building AI Agent Mobile App for DisciplinedOS

messages.content:
i think i have a big ask: Can you take a look at my repo coolgeekme/DisciplinedOS and figure out whether or not it would be possible to build a native iOS and Android mobile app where the user would use the app like an AI Agent in regards to communicating like texting or voice chat and the app would be able to determine whether or not the contents/context of that communication exchange would be worth entering into the Disciplined OS platform?

Basically, I'm looking for a true personal and professional Chief of Staff AI Agent where the user can communicate anything and then be able to log into DisciplinedOS.com and view the important information based on what the Chief of Staff deemend important.

Does that make sense?
Makes total sense — you're describing a capture layer (chat/voice agent) that feeds a curated system-of-record (DisciplinedOS). Let me look at the repo first to see what we're working with.

Yes — it makes complete sense, and after digging through the repo I have good news: **this is very feasible, and you're closer than you probably think.** The backend is already ~70% of an agent platform. Here's my assessment.

## What DisciplinedOS already has (this is the big deal)

I cloned it to `~/DisciplinedOS-inspect` and traced the server code:

- **A full AI function-calling surface** — `server/ai-tools.ts` (1,600 lines) already defines ~30 agent tools: `create_task`, `create_idea`, `create_lead`, `create_contact`, `create_note`, `create_deal`, `record_payment`, `search_across_all`, etc. This *is* the "Chief of Staff hands" — the machinery that writes deemed-important info into the platform already exists.
- **AI quick-add** — `POST /api/quick-add` (routes.ts:5786) already does natural-language → classified entity creation.
- **Voice pipeline** — `POST /api/voice-transcribe` + audio upload endpoints with Whisper transcription and GPT summaries → notes. The "talk to it" path exists server-side.
- **Token-based API auth** — Firebase Auth with Bearer ID tokens (`firebaseAuth.ts`). That's exactly what a mobile app needs; no session/cookie rework required.
- **AI insights scanning** (`aiInsightsService.ts`) — the seed of the "what's important" judgment layer.

So the ask isn't "build an AI agent platform" — it's **build a mobile capture client + a triage brain on top of an agent backend that already exists.**

## What's missing (the actual build)

**1. The mobile app itself.** My strong recommendation: **React Native (Expo)**, not separate Swift/Kotlin apps. Your stack is already TypeScript/React, Firebase Auth has first-class RN support, you get iOS + Android from one codebase, native mic/push/background audio, and Expo's EAS handles App Store/Play Store builds. "True native" x2 codebases would double cost for zero user-visible benefit here. (A cheaper stopgap — Capacitor-wrapping the existing PWA — gets you in the stores fast but makes the conversational/voice ... [truncated]
I would love you to sketch the CoS triage endpoint design against the actual schema
Let me look at the actual schema and the quick-add/ai-tools internals so the design matches reality.

I traced the real internals — key facts the design leans on:

- `storage` is **Firestore** (`storage.ts:2130` → `export const storage = firebaseStorage`); the Drizzle schema is the type layer. So "new tables" = new Firestore collections + types in `shared/schema.ts`.
- `executeAITool(toolName, args, userId)` in `ai-tools.ts:745` is already a clean, user-scoped dispatcher — the CoS can call it directly, zero duplication.
- `callOpenAIWithLogging(...)` gives you per-feature cost tracking for free in the admin dashboard.
- `aiInsights` already has `isDismissed` / `isActioned` / `relatedEntityType` / `relatedEntityId` — which means **the review-inbox storage already exists**.

Here's the sketch:

---

## CoS Triage Endpoint — Design

### New file: `server/chiefOfStaff.ts`, mounted in `routes.ts`

```
POST /api/cos/message            ← the main endpoint
GET  /api/cos/captures?status=pending
POST /api/cos/captures/:id/confirm
POST /api/cos/captures/:id/dismiss
```

All behind the existing `isAuthenticated` (Firebase Bearer token → `req.user.uid`), so the mobile app auths exactly like the PWA.

### Request / Response

```ts
// POST /api/cos/message
{
  conversationId?: string,   // omit → creates one (reuses existing conversations/messages collections)
  text?: string,             // OR:
  recordingId?: string       // voice path: app hits /api/voice-transcribe first, passes transcript through
}

// Response
{
  conversationId: string,
  reply: string,                      // conversational answer — it's still a chat
  captures: [{
    id: string,
    action: "created" | "updated" | "proposed",
    entityType: "task" | "idea" | "lead" | "contact" | "note" | "deal_activity" | "contact_note",
    entityId?: string,                // set when auto-executed
    title: string,                    // "Task: Follow up with Rogers RV on invoice"
    significance: number,             // 0–1
    sourceExcerpt: string             // the sentence(s) that triggered it
  }]
}
```

The `c... [truncated]

I was already in the process of building a mobile app, can you take a look and see how we can improve it to fit the idea of having a Chief of Staff in your pocket? 

Here is the repo of the current mobile app build: coolgeekme/disciplined-hustle-pulse
Env var didn't persist — re-exporting:

Took a good look. Honest assessment first, because the answer matters for where we go next: **this repo isn't a mobile app yet, and it's currently a different product than the Chief of Staff vision.** Here's what's actually there:

## What `disciplined-hustle-pulse` is today

- **"Pulse" — a Next.js 15 web app**, single page (`src/app/page.tsx`): enter a task → 25-min focus timer → confetti + random reward → repeat. A "Dopamine Dashboard." Clean, well-scoped, tests included — it's a nice motivational micro-app.
- **No mobile layer** — no React Native, no Expo, no Capacitor. It's a website (installable as a bookmark at best; there's no PWA manifest/service worker either).
- **No backend, no auth, no persistence** — all state is React `useState`; your stats vanish on refresh. Zero connection to DisciplinedOS.
- **No chat or voice** — nothing agent-shaped yet.
- **Stray template code**: `src/components/dashboard/` + `src/lib/mock-data.ts` are a *tennis clinic* dashboard (lessons, courts, clinics, player activity) on mock data — looks like leftovers from a template or another project. Dead weight; nothing imports mock-data except those components, and `page.tsx` doesn't render them.

So the gap to "Chief of Staff in your pocket" isn't an improvement list — it's a re-founding of the app around a different core loop, keeping Pulse as a feature.

## How I'd reshape it

**1. The core loop flips: chat is home, not the timer.** A CoS app opens to a conversation ("What's up, boss?" + today's 3 priorities pulled from DisciplinedOS), with a persistent mic button. Pulse's focus timer becomes a *tab* — and it gets better in the process, because "Lock in for 25 minutes on **Fix Eva's checkout page**" can pull real tasks from DisciplinedOS instead of free-typed text, and completed sessions can write back (task → done, hustle score credit). The dopamine loop stays; it just gets real data.

**2. The platform decision — you have three routes:**

| Route | What it gets you | Cost |

messages.content: i'm trying to add a collaborator to coolgeekme/soulprint2, but i dont want them to be able to touch or make any changes to 'main' branch. can you set that up for me?

This is a GitHub repo administration task (branch protection settings), not something I can do through code tools here — it requires access to your GitHub repo settings via the web UI or `gh` CLI with your authenticated account.

Here's how to set it up so a collaborator can't touch `main` but can still contribute:

**1. Add the collaborator with restricted permissions**
Go to `coolgeekme/soulprint2` → Settings → Collaborators and teams → Add people. Give them **Write** access (not Admin/Maintain) — this alone doesn't stop them from pushing to main, so you need step 2.

**2. Add a branch protection rule on `main`**
Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule → branch name pattern `main`:
- Enable "Require a pull request before merging"
- Enable "Require approvals" (set to at least 1) — this means their PRs need your approval to merge
- Optionally check "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" so it applies to everyone, including admins
- You can also enable "Restrict who can push to matching branches" and simply not add the collaborator to that list — this blocks direct pushes to `main` entirely, forcing them through PRs

With this setup, the collaborator can push branches and open PRs, but cannot push directly to or merge into `main` without your review/approval.

Do you want me to run the `gh` CLI commands to configure this for you (add collaborator + branch protection), or would you rather do it through the GitHub UI yourself?

I need to flag something important before continuing. The page shows this warning:

> ⚠️ **Your rules won't be enforced on this private repository until you move to a GitHub Team or Enterprise organization account.**

This means classic branch protection rules **won't actually take effect** on a private repo under a Free-tier personal account — you'd configure the rule, but it wouldn't block anything. GitHub restricts branch protection enforcement on private repos to paid Team/Enterprise plans.

Your options:
1. **Upgrade** the account/org to GitHub Team ($4/user/mo) or Enterprise so protection rules are enforced.
2. **Make the repo public** — protection rules are enforced on public repos regardless of plan (not viable if this is proprietary code, which it looks like it is from the README).
3. **Skip branch protection and just control permissions instead** — add whiteboynick with only **Read** or **Triage** access (no push access at all), so he literally cannot push to any branch, only view/comment. This achieves your goal without needing paid protection rules, though it also means he can't push to *any* branch, not just main.

[Thinking: The user is asking for a workaround since branch protection rules require a paid plan. Without those rules, GitHub's native permissions are repo-wide rather than branch-specific, so I can't restrict w]

Short answer: not reliably, on a free-tier private repo. GitHub's collaborator permissions are repo-wide, not branch-scoped — "Write" access lets someone push to *any* branch, not just one you designate. Restricting pushes to specific branches only (the "Restrict who can push to matching branches" rule) is part of branch protection, which — as we just saw — isn't enforced on private repos without a paid Team/Enterprise plan.

**The standard free workaround: use forking instead of collaborator access.**

1. Enable forking on the private repo (Settings → General → "Allow forking of this repository")
2. Give whiteboynick **Read** access only (not Write) — just enough to fork and view
3. He forks the repo to his own account and pushes freely to branches in *his fork* — he can create/modify anything there, but it's not your repo
4. When ready, he opens a pull request from his fork's branch into your `main`
5. You review and merge yourself — he has zero ability to push directly to your `main` or any other branch in your actual repo

This gets you exactly what you want (he can work freely, but can never touch your `main`) without needing a paid plan.

[Thinking: Looking at GitHub's permission model, the standard roles—Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin—don't offer branch-level granularity. Write access is the minimum needed to push any branches, but it ]

No — GitHub doesn't have a permission level that splits it that way. The collaborator roles are: **Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, Admin**, and none of them are branch-scoped. **Write** is the minimum role that allows creating/pushing branches at all — and Write also allows pushing directly to `main` (and merging PRs into it) unless a branch protection rule restricts that. There's no "Write, but not to this one branch" role built into collaborator permissions.

So practically, you have two real options:

1. **Fork workflow (free, works now)** — give him **Read** access, enable forking, he pushes to branches in his own fork and opens PRs into your `main`. He never gets push access to your repo's branches at all, including any he "creates" — those live in his fork, not yours.
2. **Write + branch protection (needs paid plan)** — give him **Write** so he can push branches directly in your repo, but add a protection rule on `main` restricting pushes/merges to just you. This is the only way to let him push branches *inside your actual repo* while `main` stays locked — and it requires upgrading to GitHub Team/Enterprise since this repo is private.

Given you want zero risk to `main` without paying for Team, the fork workflow is the one that actually works today. Want me to set that up?

- **Shorter cache TTL for misses**: unverified/not-found places cache for 1 hour instead of 7 days, so a bad venue gets rechecked sooner.

## Summary

**Root cause found**: In [server.py](backend/server.py), `PATCH /listings/{lid}/external-sources/{sid}/folders` (called when the seller saves their folder selection in the picker modal) only ever *added* newly matched files on top of whatever was already mirrored — it never removed anything. Since the "Sync now" button is available immediately after Box OAuth completes (before any folder is picked), a seller who syncs before picking folders pulls the entire drive root. Picking a specific folder afterward then just adds to that pile without ever removing the out-of-scope files — so no matter which folder is chosen, everything from that first sync stays visible.

**Fix**: folder selection is now authoritative — the PATCH endpoint wipes all previously mirrored files for that source (reusing the existing `_wipe_external_source_files` soft-delete/GridFS-cleanup used on disconnect) before triggering the fresh, scoped sync.

I opened [PR #3](https://github.com/coolgeekme/workzventures/pull/3) on branch `fix/box-folder-selection-scoping`, including a regression test. Note: I couldn't run the test suite in this sandbox (no MongoDB available), so I verified the change via `py_compile` and by tracing it against the existing test suite — the PR's test plan flags manual verification as still needed before merge.
i will test

I looked at your actual Goose setup (Extensions + Provider Configuration) rather than guessing — here's what's already there and what I'd add.

**What's already working:**
- **GitHub** — the "GitHub" extension is installed and enabled, using `api.githubcopilot.com/mcp` (GitHub's official remote MCP server, OAuth-based). This is done — it gives Goose repo/issue/PR access under your GitHub OAuth session.
- **Gmail** — "Composio Google + Search" extension is installed and enabled (hosted MCP via `backend.composio.dev`). Composio does Gmail via Google OAuth per-account — click its gear icon and connect each Gmail address separately; it supports multiple accounts.
- **Models** — you're currently on `gpt-4o` (OpenAI, API key). You also have **ChatGPT Codex** connected via OAuth (Plus/Pro subscription, no key), plus LM Studio/Local Inference running locally.

**Filling the gaps you asked about:**

1. **OAuth for models, API keys as fallback** — in Settings → Models → Configure Providers, prefer these OAuth entries over key-based ones:
   - **Gemini** — "Sign in with your Google account — no API key needed." Not yet connected; worth adding as a free, capable option.
   - **GitHub Copilot** — OAuth via your Copilot subscription, gives you Claude/GPT/Gemini models depending on your plan.
   - For Claude specifically, Goose's plain "Anthropic" card is API-key-only (I checked — no OAuth toggle there). If you want Claude via subscription instead of a key, look for the Claude Code/ACP adapter card in that same list (marked as the non-deprecated successor to "Claude Code").
   - Anything without an OAuth option (Anthropic, Mistral, etc.) — use an API key, stored in the OS keychain, which Goose does automatically.

2. **Auto-picking "the best model per inquiry"** — Goose itself doesn't have a built-in classifier for this, but two real options exist instead of building one from scratch:
   - **OpenRouter** or **Tetrate Agent Router Service** (both listed in your Provider Configuration screen) — set one of these as your provider and it automatically routes each request to the best underlying model. This is the closest match to what you described, and only needs one API key.
   - **DIY with a Goose Skill/Recipe** — you already have the "Summon" extension enabled ("delegate tasks to subagents"). You could write a Skill that triages incoming requests (e.g., "Gmail triage → cheap/fast model," "GitHub/code work → strongest coding model") and delegates via Summon. More control, more setup.

**My recommendation:** don't build a custom router yet — wire up OpenRouter as a second provider option first (five minutes, one key) and see if its auto-routing meets the bar. If it's not smart enough about your specific split (email vs. code), then it's worth building the Skill-based triage on top of Summon.

| Collection | Purpose | Powers mockup |

Here's the full picture, consolidated:

## Workflow (end-to-end)

1. Visitor lands on `teardown.coolgeek.me`, enters their URL + email, picks a tier ($49/$99).
2. Browser calls `/api/checkout` → creates a Stripe Checkout session → redirects to Stripe's hosted payment page.
3. Buyer pays → Stripe redirects them to `/success` and, separately, fires a `checkout.session.completed` webhook to `/api/webhook`.
4. The webhook handler: scrapes the target URL's HTML → sends it to Claude with a structured teardown prompt → gets back JSON findings → renders it into a PDF → emails the PDF via Resend to the buyer.
5. You track sales in the Stripe dashboard (no separate analytics needed at this stage).

Nothing here needs you to touch anything manually per-sale — it's fully automated once the keys below are in place.

## APIs / accounts needed (in the order you'll set them up)

| Service | What it's for | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|
| **Stripe** | Checkout + webhook | Secret key from dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys; webhook signing secret from the endpoint you create pointing at `https://teardown.coolgeek.me/api/webhook` |
| **Anthropic API key** | Generates the actual teardown content | console.anthropic.com → Create Key (billed separately from any Claude.ai subscription, pay-per-token) |
| **Resend** | Emails the PDF to the buyer | resend.com → API key + verify `teardown.coolgeek.me` as a sending domain (adds a couple more DNS TXT records in GoDaddy) |

That's it — no other APIs required. Once you hand me those three, I'll wire them into Vercel's environment variables and we can test a real $1 test-mode payment before going live.

Per the "organic only, zero budget" plan:

1. **X/Twitter** — a build-in-public account for the product (e.g. `@teardownhq` or similar, whatever's available). Used for proof-of-work posts and replying in founder threads.
2. **Reddit** — just your existing personal account is fine; no dedicated brand account needed (branded accounts read as spam in r/SaaS, r/startups etc. — replies should look like a person, not a company).
3. **IndieHackers** — a profile under your own name or a product-branded one, whichever you're more comfortable posting under; IH tolerates "building X" posts from founder accounts well.

Nothing else needed — no Instagram/TikTok/LinkedIn for this particular offer, since the buyer niche (SaaS/indie founders) lives on X, Reddit, and IndieHackers, not those other platforms.

Good — I now have a clear picture. Here's my diagnosis.

## What I found

I cloned `coolgeekme/videokinetix` and checked out Codex's `feature/persistent-athlete-tracking` branch (15+ commits). The commit history itself is a signal: *"Harden athlete lock and reacquisition," "Prevent tracking switches during occlusion," "Keep athlete lock through fast motion," "Keep athlete lock through shooting motion"* — repeated patches at the same symptom. That pattern usually means a structural problem, not a missing tweak, and reading the code confirmed it.

**Root cause: there are two competing trackers instead of one source of truth.**

1. A backend Supervision + Roboflow BoT-SORT tracker (`backend/tracking_service.py`) — real, correctly wired into `server.py`. It receives detections over an HTTP POST roughly every 140ms (JPEG-encode → multipart upload → server inference → response).
2. A separate, hand-rolled client-side tracker (`frontend/src/lib/poseIdentityTracker.js`) that re-derives identity every single frame (~30ms) from MediaPipe pose landmarks using its own IOU/velocity/shape heuristics.

[PoseCanvas.jsx:1337-1379](frontend/src/components/PoseCanvas.jsx:1337) reconciles these two asynchronous, disagreeing opinions every tick with a hand-tuned scoring formula (`similarity * 2.5 - distance * 2`, cutoffs at 0.34/0.38/0.3). When the fast local heuristic and the slow, network-jittery server opinion disagree — which is often, because BoT-SORT's `minimum_iou_threshold_first_assoc` is set to a very permissive `0.08` — the code has to guess who's right. Each "athlete lock" bug report has been fixed by adding another special case to that reconciliation logic, which is why the same class of bug keeps resurfacing in a new shape. Supervision itself isn't the problem; it's fighting a race it can't win.

**Second finding, maybe the bigger opportunity:** even in "upload" mode (reviewing an already-recorded clip — likely the primary basketball/swim review workflow), the app still re-plays the video in real time and streams frames live to the tracker one at a time, instead of processing the whole file server-side in one batch pass. For a file that's already fully available, that's giving up Supervision's actual strength (offline, full-framerate, no network jitter, `sv.get_video_frames_generator` + ByteTrack/BoT-SORT run once) for no reason.

## Proposed plan

- **Phase 1 (tactical, days not weeks):** make the backend BoT-SORT track the single authority once it's available; stop the client heuristic from overriding it, tighten the IOU thresholds, keep the client tracker only as a same-frame bridge during the ~140ms gap.
- **Phase 2 (bigger lift, likely the largest accuracy win):** for upload-mode review, replace the live frame-streaming with a one-shot backend batch job — process the whole clip with Supervision + BoT-SORT at full framerate, return a per-frame track manifest, and have the frontend just play it back in sync. This removes network jitter and dropped-frame issues entirely for that workflow.

Since Phase 2 is a real architecture change (new batch endpoint, async job handling, frontend playback rewrite) and a bigger time investment than Phase 1, I'd like your call on scope before I start burning hours on it.

## Done — pushed to `claude/tracking-batch-authority`

**Root cause found:** the backend Supervision/BoT-SORT tracker was only ever a soft advisory signal into a much older, hand-tuned per-frame heuristic in [PoseCanvas.jsx](frontend/src/components/PoseCanvas.jsx) that actually decided "who is the athlete" every frame (distance + appearance-histogram + torso-scale + ~10 magic-number thresholds). That's why Codex's 15+ commits kept patching the symptom without it converging — Supervision's answer was never authoritative.

**What I shipped, on `claude/tracking-batch-authority` (branched off Codex's `feature/persistent-athlete-tracking`, not `main`, so it won't collide with any work still in progress there):**

- `POST /api/tracking/batch` in [tracking_service.py](backend/tracking_service.py) — runs BoT-SORT once over a whole clip's frames with no real-time deadline, using a stricter threshold profile (`BOT_SORT_BATCH_OPTIONS`) than the live 7fps path, since dense sampling no longer needs the loose IOU gates that caused crossing basketball players to swap IDs.
- [videoTrackingManifest.js](frontend/src/lib/videoTrackingManifest.js) — seeks through an uploaded clip once, submits every frame's detections in one batch call, and returns a manifest the render loop can look up by playback time.
- A minimal, surgical splice in [PoseCanvas.jsx](frontend/src/components/PoseCanvas.jsx): when a manifest is ready (upload/review mode), skip the live 140ms network call and feed the same existing reconciliation logic from the manifest lookup instead. Live webcam capture is untouched.

**Verified:** all 17 backend pytest cases + 40 frontend Jest tests pass (new coverage added). `npm run build` fails, but on a pre-existing, unrelated `ajv`/`ajv-keywords` version conflict in `react-scripts`'s own dependency tree — confirmed via `npm ls`, nothing to do with this diff.

**What I can't verify from here:** whether lock actually holds better on real basketball/swim footage — that needs a human (or Codex) in an actual browser with real clips. The [README](README.md) already documents the local dev-server setup for that.

Pushed to `claude/tracking-batch-authority` (commit `4215ca4`).

## What I found

The bug lives in `start()`'s rewind path in [PoseCanvas.jsx](frontend/src/components/PoseCanvas.jsx). When "Start Capture" is pressed after previewing the clip (commonly: watching it play through to confirm the lock holds, then hitting Start — which triggers `getCapturePlaybackPlan`'s rewind since you're near the end), the code resets several tracking caches but **never resets the local pose tracker's internal state** (`poseTrackerRef.current`). That tracker's one track stays anchored at wherever the athlete was *before* the rewind. After the seek, it can never legitimately re-match — and the existing appearance-based recovery mechanism (built for "edited clips can teleport the athlete") explicitly skips ROI-mode targets, which is exactly what a fixed-camera swimmer (or a small/far athlete) selected without a BoT-SORT box uses.

Net effect: `targetIdx` stays `-1` for the rest of the capture. The skeleton/identity indicator can still look fine visually in some cases, but every recorded frame is empty, so rep detection has nothing to work with — matching "identity locks during preview, pose landmarks/rep tracking stop after Start."

## What I fixed

1. Reset `poseTrackerRef` on rewind so the first post-rewind frame starts clean instead of carrying a stale, unmatchable track.
2. Added a scoped flag (`awaitingRewindReacquireRef`) that lets the appearance-based reacquisition path also run for ROI-mode targets, but *only* in the window right after a rewind — normal playback behavior for swimming/small-athlete ROI targets is unchanged.
3. Added a one-time console warning if a capture ever finishes its first frame with zero usable poses, dumping the exact identity/appearance/ROI state — so if this resurfaces, the next report comes with real signal instead of another guessing round.

Verified: all 58 frontend Jest tests still pass, and I babel-compiled `PoseCanvas.jsx` directly to confirm no syntax errors (there's no direct unit test for this component, so that's the extent of what I could verify without a browser + real footage).

**One thing I want to confirm with you:** did your repro involve previewing the clip through to (or near) the end before pressing Start? That's the specific path this fix addresses. If your repro starts capture from *mid-clip* with no rewind, this fix won't touch it, and the diagnostic log I added will tell us why on your next test in Codex — check the console for `[PoseCanvas] recording has not captured a usable pose yet`.

**Root cause: two competing copies of the app, and the old one is broken.**

This repo started as a Google AI Studio single-file export (see `README.md`: *"Run and deploy your AI Studio app"*), then got migrated to a proper `frontend/` + `backend/` split (matching your `playerscoutsai` pattern) — but the original AI Studio files were never deleted. They're just sitting at the repo root alongside the real app:

- It's also stale: last touched 2026-01-23, while the real app in `frontend/`+`backend/` was last touched 2026-05-07 — four months more current.
- The root's `services/geminiService.ts` calls Gemini **directly from the browser** with the API key inlined client-side — the exact anti-pattern the `frontend/`+`backend/` split was built to fix (their `backend/scouting.py` proxies Gemini server-side instead).
- There's also a `varsityscout-ai.zip` committed at the root — it's literally a zip of that same original AI Studio export (confirmed by unzipping it), unreferenced by anything.

Having two `package.json`/`vite.config.ts` at different directory depths is exactly the kind of thing that confuses a platform's auto-detection during build/deploy — this is a very plausible source of whatever error you're seeing.

`.env`, `.env.local`, `backend/.env`, and `frontend/.env` are all committed to git with live values (a Gemini API key, and a MongoDB connection string). topics.name: Claude: Convert athleteedgeai.com to platform hub

messages.content:
I have a domain athleteeddgeai.com and i'm not really doing anything with it. When i first bought it, my plan was to build a resource for athletes...like having an AI basketball trainer, a pb coach, nutritionist, etc.

Now, i'm thinking athleteedgeai.com should be more of a "hub" where I can share my sports related platforms: playtrackr.app, varsityscoutai.com, playerscoutsai.com, visionkinetix.ai, pbcoach.app

What do you think?

[Thinking: This is a strategic question about consolidating sports platform domains into a hub rather than a technical implementation task. I should provide a focused recommendation with the key tradeoff in mind]

A "hub" is a reasonable way to get some use out of an idle domain, but I'd flag one tradeoff: **athleteedgeai.com** signals a specific AI product to a visitor, not a portfolio page — so people landing there expecting "AI basketball trainer" will bounce when they hit a list of links instead. If those five products (playtrackr, varsityscoutai, playerscoutsai, visionkinetix, pbcoach) don't share a brand identity or target the same user, the hub may not drive much cross-traffic between them either — it just becomes a resume of your projects rather than a growth lever for any one of them.

If the real goal is "don't waste the domain," a simpler high-value use might be a single AI-agent tool that lives up to the name (even a scoped one, like a rep-counting or PR-tracking tool) that also cross-links your other products — that gets you both an active asset and the hub benefit. Want me to sketch out what a hub page vs. a scoped-tool approach would actually look like for this domain?

I read through the full 6-page document (it's Dick's Sporting Goods' standard arbitration agreement, since GameChanger is a DSG subsidiary). Here's a plain-language summary.

## What it is
A pre-dispute agreement that requires you and Dick's Sporting Goods (parent company of GameChanger) to resolve almost all employment-related disputes through **binding arbitration instead of a court or jury trial** — for the entire application process and, if hired, your employment there.

## What's covered (very broad)
Essentially any dispute connected to your application, hiring, or employment: wrongful termination, discrimination, harassment, retaliation, wage/hour issues (overtime, off-the-clock, commissions), breach of contract, and claims under most major federal employment laws (Title VII, ADA, ADEA, FMLA, FLSA, etc.).

## What's carved out (rights you keep regardless)
- Workers' comp, unemployment, and state disability benefit claims
- Filing with government agencies — EEOC, Department of Labor, NLRB, OSHA, etc. — is still fully available; arbitration doesn't block you from reporting to a regulator
- Sexual harassment/sexual assault claims (arising after March 2022) — you can specifically opt out of arbitrating *those*, but you have to elect that within 30 days of receiving an arbitration demand

## How arbitration actually works
- A single arbitrator (must be a retired federal/state judge) hears the case, under JAMS rules
- Company pays the arbitrator's fees and any arbitration-specific costs beyond what a court filing fee would cost you
- Each side pays its own attorney fees, unless the law would have allowed fee-shifting in court anyway
- The arbitrator's decision is **final and essentially unappealable** (only very narrow exceptions under federal law)

## The two provisions that matter most
1. **No class or collective actions.** You waive the right to join a class action or bring a representative claim (including PAGA) — you can only bring claims as yourself, individually. This is the single biggest right you'd be giving up.
2. **It applies whether or not you check the box.** The document says explicitly: even if you don't accept/sign, simply continuing to apply for or work at the company binds you to it anyway. So declining the checkbox doesn't actually opt you out if you proceed with the application.

## One more detail
It survives after employment ends — it doesn't expire when you leave the company.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

generate a prompt i can use for another model to create an artifact like this QA page.

[Thinking: I need to create a prompt that another AI can use to build a similar QA page—something comprehensive and self-contained that captures the structure, design, and content strategy we developed, but gene]

Here's a self-contained prompt you can hand to another model (ChatGPT, Gemini, another Claude session, etc.) to reproduce this kind of artifact. It's templated with bracketed placeholders so you can reuse it for other projects later.

---

```
You are building an interactive QA test plan as a single self-contained HTML file for a real person to execute against a live product over multiple days. Treat this as a working tool, not a document — it needs to survive being reloaded, filled in over a week, and handed back with evidence attached.

CONTEXT
- Product/repo to test: [REPO OR PRODUCT NAME, e.g. "github.com/org/repo"]
- Source material to ground tasks in: [e.g. "the repo's route table, API router mounts, README, changelog, and any PRD/feature docs — read the actual code, don't invent features]
- Timeframe: spread across [N] days, roughly [X] hours/day
- Tester's access level and constraints: [e.g. "no platform/staff admin access — exclude anything requiring it"; "no real client credentials, only test/throwaway accounts"; list anything else out of scope]
- Any known fragile areas to flag: [e.g. "pull recent bug-fix history from CHANGELOG.md and mark those areas as regression risks"]

RESEARCH FIRST
Before writing anything, actually investigate the source material — read the real routes/endpoints, the real recent bug history, and any docs describing shipped vs. in-progress features. If two docs disagree about whether something has shipped, flag the discrepancy rather than picking one silently. Every checklist item should map to something that actually exists and is wired up live, not something you're inferring might exist.

STRUCTURE
- Group the plan into [N] day-sized sections, each building logically on the previous day's setup (e.g. accounts/data created on day 1 get reused all week, not recreated).
- Each day gets:
  - A short "hands-on task" — one concrete, realistic scenario a tester actually performs (not "check that X works" but "build a real deliverable that exercises X, Y, and Z together").
  - A checklist of granular items below it, each with:
    - A clear pass/fail label
    - An explicit "Steps:" line — exact clicks/inputs/navigation and exactly what result counts as a pass, written so someone unfamiliar with the product can execute it without guessing
    - A route/endpoint tag if applicable
- Include a "Before you start" section up front listing exactly what access/credentials/accounts are needed and by which day, so the tester is never blocked mid-week waiting on something they should have asked for earlier.
- Include a "week at a glance" table up top with clickable jump-links to each day.
- Mark any item that depends on access the tester doesn't have as fully out of scope (remove it, don't just leave it unchecked) rather than leaving ambiguous dead weight.
- Tag items that were recently broken/fixed (regression risk) distinctly from items that span multiple days (e.g. "scheduled on day 2, verify it fired on day 3").

INTERACTIVITY (this must actually work, not just look interactive)
- Every checklist item is a real checkbox with a visible progress counter (checked/total) that updates live.
- Every item supports a free-text note field and an attached screenshot (click-to-browse AND paste-from-clipboard), so the tester can document exactly what happened on a failure.
- Compress pasted/uploaded screenshots client-side (canvas resize + JPEG re-encode) before storing, so you don't blow past browser storage limits.
- Persist all state (checked/note/screenshot) to localStorage so a reload doesn't lose progress.
- Add a small visual indicator on any item that has a note or screenshot attached, so nothing gets lost in a long list.
- Since this is a static file with no backend, be explicit in an on-page instructions section that nothing syncs anywhere automatically — provide an "Export report" action that compiles everything (status + notes + screenshot thumbnails) into a document the tester can copy or download and send back manually. Don't let the tool imply it reports back on its own.
- A reset action should require a confirm-by-clicking-twice pattern rather than a native browser confirm() dialog, since those can be blocked in sandboxed preview environments.

DESIGN
- One self-contained HTML file: inline CSS and JS, no external requests, no CDN fonts.
- Support both light and dark mode via CSS custom properties, reacting to prefers-color-scheme and an explicit data-theme override.
- Pick a deliberate, non-generic color palette and type pairing appropriate to the subject — avoid default AI-generated looks (cream+terracotta+serif, purple gradient hero, emoji section markers, Inter-everywhere).
- Numbered day structure is justified here since it's a genuine sequence — use it, but don't add numbering elsewhere unless it encodes real order.

CRITICAL TECHNICAL CONSTRAINT
Do not use literal "smart" typographic characters (em dashes, en dashes, curly quotes, ellipsis, arrows, multiplication signs, etc.) anywhere in the raw file. Depending on how the file gets served, these can get charset-mangled into garbled text. Use HTML entities (—, →, etc.) in markup, and JavaScript \u escape sequences (e.g. "\u2014") for any of these characters inside <script> tags, since HTML entities do NOT decode inside script blocks and will otherwise appear as literal garbage text. The entire file should be pure ASCII except where entities/escapes are used.

OUTPUT
Produce the complete HTML file, ready to open directly in a browser with no build step.
```

---

A few notes on why I included what I did: the "critical technical constraint" section exists because I actually hit that exact mojibake bug while building yours, and it's a subtle enough failure mode that most models won't catch it unprompted. The "remove rather than leave unchecked" and "before you start" guidance both came directly from your feedback in this conversation. Swap the bracketed placeholders for your next project and it should produce something structurally similar.

## Yes — the inquiry form does send a "thank you" email

Here's how it works in [emporio_zeva](https://github.com/coolgeekme/emporio_zeva):

1. **Submission**: `POST /api/inquiries` (backend/server.py:741-747) saves the inquiry to MongoDB, then fires `emailer.notify_inquiry()` as a background task.
2. **Customer auto-reply**: In [backend/emailer.py:139-159](), if the submitter provided an email, it sends them a branded email titled **"Your note reached Eva"** with copy like:
   > "Thank you, {name}. Your note has reached me. I read every inquiry personally and will reply within a day or two..." — signed "Eva"

   It also echoes back their submitted message and sends a separate internal notification email to the ops inbox (`RESEND_NOTIFY_TO`).

**One caveat worth flagging**: emails are sent via Resend, and the send function fails silently if not configured (`backend/emailer.py:36-43,77-84`) — this is intentional so a broken mail provider never blocks form submission. But `render.yaml` (the deploy blueprint) doesn't provision `RESEND_API_KEY`, `RESEND_FROM`, or `RESEND_NOTIFY_TO` as env vars, and neither `DEPLOY_RENDER.md` nor `README.md` mention setting them up. So on a fresh Render deploy following just the blueprint, the thank-you email logic exists and is wired in, but **won't actually send anything** until someone manually adds a `RESEND_API_KEY` (and ideally `RESEND_NOTIFY_TO`) in the Render dashboard. Worth checking whether that's already been set for the live deployment.

# Product Marketing Context

You help users create and maintain a product marketing context document. This captures foundational positioning and messaging information that other marketing skills reference, so users don't repeat themselves.

The document is stored at `.agents/product-marketing.md`.

## Workflow

### Step 1: Check for Existing Context

First, check if `.agents/product-marketing.md` already exists. Also check `.claude/product-marketing.md` and the legacy filename `product-marketing-context.md` (in either `.agents/` or `.claude/`) for older setups — if found anywhere other than `.agents/product-marketing.md`, offer to move it to the canonical location.

**If it exists:**
- Read it and summarize what's captured
- Ask which sections they want to update
- Only gather info for those sections

**If it doesn't exist, offer two options:**

1. **Auto-draft from codebase** (recommended): You'll study the repo—README, landing pages, marketing copy, package.json, etc.—and draft a V1 of the context document. The user then reviews, corrects, and fills gaps. This is faster than starting from scratch.

2. **Start from scratch**: Walk through each section conversationally, gathering info one section at a time.

Most users prefer option 1. After presenting the draft, ask: "What needs correcting? What's missing?"

### Step 2: Gather Information

**If auto-drafting:**
1. Read the codebase: README, landing pages, marketing copy, about pages, meta descriptions, package.json, any existing docs
2. Draft all sections based on what you find
3. Present the draft and ask what needs correcting or is missing
4. Iterate until the user is satisfied

**If starting from scratch:**
Walk through each section below conversationally, one at a time. Don't dump all questions at once.

For each section:
1. Briefly explain what you're capturing
2. Ask relevant questions
3. Confirm accuracy
4. Move to the next

Push for verbatim customer language — exact phrases are more valuable than polished descriptions because they reflect how customers actually think and speak, which makes copy more resonant.

---

## Sections to Capture

### 1. Product Overview
- One-line description
- What it does (2-3 sentences)
- Product category (what "shelf" you sit on—how customers search for you)
- Product type (SaaS, marketplace, e-commerce, service, etc.)
- Business model and pricing

### 2. Target Audience
- Target company type (industry, size, stage)
- Target decision-makers (roles, departments)
- Primary use case (the main problem you solve)
- Jobs to be done (2-3 things customers "hire" you for)
- Specific use cases or scenarios

### 3. Personas (B2B only)
If multiple stakeholders are involved in buying, capture for each:
- User, Champion, Decision Maker, Financial Buyer, Technical Influencer
- What each cares about, their challenge, and the value you promise them

### 4. Problems & Pain Points
- Core challenge customers face before finding you
- Why current solutions fall short
- What it costs them (time, money, opportunities)
- Emotional tension (stress, fear, doubt)

### 5. Competitive Landscape
- **Direct competitors**: Same solution, same problem (e.g., Calendly vs SavvyCal)
- **Secondary competitors**: Different solution, same problem (e.g., Calendly vs Superhuman scheduling)
- **Indirect competitors**: Conflicting approach (e.g., Calendly vs personal assistant)
- How each falls short for customers

### 6. Differentiation
- Key differentiators (capabilities alternatives lack)
- How you solve it differently
- Why that's better (benefits)
- Why customers choose you over alternatives

### 7. Objections & Anti-Personas
- Top 3 objections heard in sales and how to address them
- Who is NOT a good fit (anti-persona)

### 8. Switching Dynamics
The JTBD Four Forces:
- **Push**: What frustrations drive them away from current solution
- **Pull**: What attracts them to you
- **Habit**: What keeps them stuck with current approach
- **Anxiety**: What worries them about switching

### 9. Customer Language
- How customers describe the problem (verbatim)
- How they describe your solution (verbatim)
- Words/phrases to use
- Words/phrases to avoid
- Glossary of product-specific terms

### 10. Brand Voice
- Tone (professional, casual, playful, etc.)
- Communication style (direct, conversational, technical)
- Brand personality (3-5 adjectives)

### 11. Proof Points
- Key metrics or results to cite
- Notable customers/logos
- Testimonial snippets
- Main value themes and supporting evidence

### 12. Goals
- Primary business goal
- Key conversion action (what you want people to do)
- Current metrics (if known)

# Content Strategy

You are a content strategist. Your goal is to help plan content that drives traffic, builds authority, and generates leads by being either searchable, shareable, or both.

## Before Planning

**Check for product marketing context first:**
If `.agents/product-marketing.md` exists (or `.claude/product-marketing.md`, or the legacy `product-marketing-context.md` filename, in older setups), read it before asking questions. Use that context and only ask for information not already covered or specific to this task.

Gather this context (ask if not provided):

### 1. Business Context
- What does the company do?
- Who is the ideal customer?
- What's the primary goal for content? (traffic, leads, brand awareness, thought leadership)
- What problems does your product solve?

### 2. Customer Research
- What questions do customers ask before buying?
- What objections come up in sales calls?
- What topics appear repeatedly in support tickets?
- What language do customers use to describe their problems?

### 3. Current State
- Do you have existing content? What's working?
- What resources do you have? (writers, budget, time)
- What content formats can you produce? (written, video, audio)

### 4. Competitive Landscape
- Who are your main competitors?
- What content gaps exist in your market?

---

## Searchable vs Shareable

Every piece of content must be searchable, shareable, or both. Prioritize in that order—search traffic is the foundation.

**Searchable content** captures existing demand. Optimized for people actively looking for answers.

**Shareable content** creates demand. Spreads ideas and gets people talking.

### When Writing Searchable Content

- Target a specific keyword or question
- Match search intent exactly—answer what the searcher wants
- Use clear titles that match search queries
- Structure with headings that mirror search patterns
- Place keywords in title, headings, first paragraph, URL
- Provide comprehensive coverage (don't leave questions unanswered)
- Include data, examples, and links to authoritative sources
- Optimize for AI/LLM discovery: clear positioning, structured content, brand consistency across the web

### When Writing Shareable Content

- Lead with a novel insight, original data, or counterintuitive take
- Challenge conventional wisdom with well-reasoned arguments
- Tell stories that make people feel something
- Create content people want to share to look smart or help others
- Connect to current trends or emerging problems
- Share vulnerable, honest experiences others can learn from

---

## Content Types

### Searchable Content Types

**Use-Case Content**
Formula: [persona] + [use-case]. Targets long-tail keywords.
- "Project management for designers"
- "Task tracking for developers"
- "Client collaboration for freelancers"

**Hub and Spoke**
Hub = comprehensive overview. Spokes = related subtopics.
```
/topic (hub)
├── /topic/subtopic-1 (spoke)
├── /topic/subtopic-2 (spoke)
└── /topic/subtopic-3 (spoke)
```
Create hub first, then build spokes. Interlink strategically.

**Note:** Most content works fine under `/blog`. Only use dedicated hub/spoke URL structures for major topics with layered depth (e.g., Atlassian's `/agile` guide). For typical blog posts, `/blog/post-title` is sufficient.

**Template Libraries**
High-intent keywords + product adoption.
- Target searches like "marketing plan template"
- Provide immediate standalone value
- Show how product enhances the template

### Shareable Content Types

**Thought Leadership**
- Articulate concepts everyone feels but hasn't named
- Challenge conventional wisdom with evidence
- Share vulnerable, honest experiences

**Data-Driven Content**
- Product data analysis (anonymized insights)
- Public data analysis (uncover patterns)
- Original research (run experiments, share results)

**Expert Roundups**
15-30 experts answering one specific question. Built-in distribution.

**Case Studies**
Structure: Challenge → Solution → Results → Key learnings

**Meta Content**
Behind-the-scenes transparency. "How We Got Our First $5k MRR," "Why We Chose Debt Over VC."

For programmatic content at scale, see **programmatic-seo** skill.

---

## Content Pillars and Topic Clusters

Content pillars are the 3-5 core topics your brand will own. Each pillar spawns a cluster of related content.

Most of the time, all content can live under `/blog` with good internal linking between related posts. Dedicated pillar pages with custom URL structures (like `/guides/topic`) are only needed when you're building comprehensive resources with multiple layers of depth.

### How to Identify Pillars

1. **Product-led**: What problems does your product solve?
2. **Audience-led**: What does your ICP need to learn?
3. **Search-led**: What topics have volume in your space?
4. **Competitor-led**: What are competitors ranking for?

### Pillar Structure

```
Pillar Topic (Hub)
├── Subtopic Cluster 1
│   ├── Article A
│   ├── Article B
│   └── Article C
├── Subtopic Cluster 2
│   ├── Article D
│   ├── Article E
│   └── Article F
└── Subtopic Cluster 3
    ├── Article G
    ├── Article H
    └── Article I
```

### Pillar Criteria

Good pillars should:
- Align with your product/service
- Match what your audience cares about
- Have search volume and/or social interest
- Be broad enough for many subtopics

---

## Keyword Research by Buyer Stage

Map topics to the buyer's journey using proven keyword modifiers:

### Awareness Stage
Modifiers: "what is," "how to," "guide to," "introduction to"

Example: If customers ask about project management basics:
- "What is Agile Project Management"
- "Guide to Sprint Planning"
- "How to Run a Standup Meeting"

### Consideration Stage
Modifiers: "best," "top," "vs," "alternatives," "comparison"

Example: If customers evaluate multiple tools:
- "Best Project Management Tools for Remote Teams"
- "Asana vs Trello vs Monday"
- "Basecamp Alternatives"

### Decision Stage
Modifiers: "pricing," "reviews," "demo," "trial," "buy"

Example: If pricing comes up in sales calls:
- "Project Management Tool Pricing Comparison"
- "How to Choose the Right Plan"
- "[Product] Reviews"

### Implementation Stage
Modifiers: "templates," "examples," "tutorial," "how to use," "setup"

Example: If support tickets show implementation struggles:
- "Project Template Library"
- "Step-by-Step Setup Tutorial"
- "How to Use [Feature]"

---

## Content Ideation Sources

### 1. Keyword Data

If user provides keyword exports (Ahrefs, SEMrush, GSC), analyze for:
- Topic clusters (group related keywords)
- Buyer stage (awareness/consideration/decision/implementation)
- Search intent (informational, commercial, transactional)
- Quick wins (low competition + decent volume + high relevance)
- Content gaps (keywords competitors rank for that you don't)

Output as prioritized table:
| Keyword | Volume | Difficulty | Buyer Stage | Content Type | Priority |

### 2. Call Transcripts

If user provides sales or customer call transcripts, extract:
- Questions asked → FAQ content or blog posts
- Pain points → problems in their own words
- Objections → content to address proactively
- Language patterns → exact phrases to use (voice of customer)
- Competitor mentions → what they compared you to

Output content ideas with supporting quotes.

### 3. Survey Responses

If user provides survey data, mine for:
- Open-ended responses (topics and language)
- Common themes (30%+ mention = high priority)
- Resource requests (what they wish existed)
- Content preferences (formats they want)

### 4. Forum Research

Use web search to find content ideas:

**Reddit:** `site:reddit.com [topic]`
- Top posts in relevant subreddits
- Questions and frustrations in comments
- Upvoted answers (validates what resonates)

**Quora:** `site:quora.com [topic]`
- Most-followed questions
- Highly upvoted answers

**Other:** Indie Hackers, Hacker News, Product Hunt, industry Slack/Discord

Extract: FAQs, misconceptions, debates, problems being solved, terminology used.

### 5. Competitor Analysis

Use web search to analyze competitor content:

**Find their content:** `site:competitor.com/blog`

**Analyze:**
- Top-performing posts (comments, shares)
- Topics covered repeatedly
- Gaps they haven't covered
- Case studies (customer problems, use cases, results)
- Content structure (pillars, categories, formats)

**Identify opportunities:**
- Topics you can cover better
- Angles they're missing
- Outdated content to improve on

### 6. Sales and Support Input

Extract from customer-facing teams:
- Common objections
- Repeated questions
- Support ticket patterns
- Success stories
- Feature requests and underlying problems

---

## Prioritizing Content Ideas

Score each idea on four factors:

### 1. Customer Impact (40%)
- How frequently did this topic come up in research?
- What percentage of customers face this challenge?
- How emotionally charged was this pain point?
- What's the potential LTV of customers with this need?

### 2. Content-Market Fit (30%)
- Does this align with problems your product solves?
- Can you offer unique insights from customer research?
- Do you have customer stories to support this?
- Will this naturally lead to product interest?

### 3. Search Potential (20%)
- What's the monthly search volume?
- How competitive is this topic?
- Are there related long-tail opportunities?
- Is search interest growing or declining?

### 4. Resource Requirements (10%)
- Do you have expertise to create authoritative content?
- What additional research is needed?
- What assets (graphics, data, examples) will you need?

### Scoring Template

| Idea | Customer Impact (40%) | Content-Market Fit (30%) | Search Potential (20%) | Resources (10%) | Total |
|------|----------------------|-------------------------|----------------------|-----------------|-------|
| Topic A | 8 | 9 | 7 | 6 | 8.0 |
| Topic B | 6 | 7 | 9 | 8 | 7.1 |

---

## Output Format

When creating a content strategy, provide:

### 1. Content Pillars
- 3-5 pillars with rationale
- Subtopic clusters for each pillar
- How pillars connect to product

### 2. Priority Topics
For each recommended piece:
- Topic/title
- Searchable, shareable, or both
- Content type (use-case, hub/spoke, thought leadership, etc.)
- Target keyword and buyer stage
- Why this topic (customer research backing)

### 3. Topic Cluster Map
Visual or structured representation of how content interconnects.

---

You are an expert social media strategist. Your goal is to help create engaging content that builds audience, drives engagement, and supports business goals.

## Before Creating Content

**Check for product marketing context first:**
If `.agents/product-marketing.md` exists (or `.claude/product-marketing.md`, or the legacy `product-marketing-context.md` filename, in older setups), read it before asking questions. Use that context and only ask for information not already covered or specific to this task.

Gather this context (ask if not provided):

### 1. Goals
- What's the primary objective? (Brand awareness, leads, traffic, community)
- What action do you want people to take?
- Are you building personal brand, company brand, or both?

### 2. Audience
- Who are you trying to reach?
- What platforms are they most active on?
- What content do they engage with?

### 3. Brand Voice
- What's your tone? (Professional, casual, witty, authoritative)
- Any topics to avoid?
- Any specific terminology or style guidelines?

### 4. Resources
- How much time can you dedicate to social?
- Do you have existing content to repurpose?
- Can you create video content?

## Platform Quick Reference

| Platform | Best For | Frequency | Key Format |
|----------|----------|-----------|------------|
| LinkedIn | B2B, thought leadership | 3-5x/week | Carousels, stories |
| Twitter/X | Tech, real-time, community | 3-10x/day | Threads, hot takes |
| Instagram | Visual brands, lifestyle | 1-2 posts + Stories daily | Reels, carousels |
| TikTok | Brand awareness, younger audiences | 1-4x/day | Short-form video |
| Facebook | Communities, local businesses | 1-2x/day | Groups, native video |

**For detailed platform strategies**: See [references/platforms.md](references/platforms.md)

**For hashtag limits and character counts**: See [references/platform-limits.md](references/platform-limits.md)

## Content Pillars Framework

Build your content around 3-5 pillars that align with your expertise and audience interests.

### Example for a SaaS Founder

| Pillar | % of Content | Topics |
|--------|--------------|--------|
| Industry insights | 30% | Trends, data, predictions |
| Behind-the-scenes | 25% | Building the company, lessons learned |
| Educational | 25% | How-tos, frameworks, tips |
| Personal | 15% | Stories, values, hot takes |
| Promotional | 5% | Product updates, offers |

### Pillar Development Questions

For each pillar, ask:
1. What unique perspective do you have?
2. What questions does your audience ask?
3. What content has performed well before?
4. What can you create consistently?
5. What aligns with business goals?

---

## Hook Formulas

The first line determines whether anyone reads the rest.

### Curiosity Hooks
- "I was wrong about [common belief]."
- "The real reason [outcome] happens isn't what you think."
- "[Impressive result] — and it only took [surprisingly short time]."

### Story Hooks
- "Last week, [unexpected thing] happened."
- "I almost [big mistake/failure]."
- "3 years ago, I [past state]. Today, [current state]."

### Value Hooks
- "How to [desirable outcome] (without [common pain]):"
- "[Number] [things] that [outcome]:"
- "Stop [common mistake]. Do this instead:"

### Contrarian Hooks
- "Unpopular opinion: [bold statement]"
- "[Common advice] is wrong. Here's why:"
- "I stopped [common practice] and [positive result]."

**For post templates and more hooks**: See [references/post-templates.md](references/post-templates.md)

**For carousels** (Instagram carousels, LinkedIn document posts): See [references/carousel-frameworks.md](references/carousel-frameworks.md) — five slide-by-slide narrative architectures (Value-Stack, Problem-Proof, Hack List, Rant Callout, Demo Walkthrough) with framework selection guidance, per-slide copy slots, platform notes, and a production checklist. Pick the framework before writing slides.

## Content Repurposing System

Turn one piece of content into many. The best social content isn't created from scratch — it's extracted from longer-form pillar content and adapted to each platform.

### Blog Post → Social Content

| Platform | Format |
|----------|--------|
| LinkedIn | Key insight + link in comments |
| LinkedIn | Carousel of main points |
| Twitter/X | Thread of key takeaways |
| Instagram | Carousel with visuals |
| Instagram | Reel summarizing the post |

### Podcast / Video → Social Content

Extract "content atoms" — self-contained moments from any long-form content that work on their own:

| Atom Type | What to Look For | Best Platform |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------|
| Quotable moment | A bold claim, hot take, or memorable line (15-60 sec) | Twitter/X, LinkedIn, TikTok |
| Story arc | A complete mini-story with setup, conflict, resolution (60-90 sec) | Instagram Reels, TikTok, YouTube Shorts |
| Tactical tip | A specific how-to or framework explained clearly (30-60 sec) | LinkedIn, YouTube Shorts |
| Controversial take | A contrarian opinion that sparks debate | Twitter/X, LinkedIn |
| Data/stat callout | A surprising number or research finding | LinkedIn carousel, Twitter/X |
| Behind-the-scenes | Authentic, unpolished moments | Instagram Stories, TikTok |

**Podcast repurposing workflow:**
1. **Get transcript** — use Whisper, Descript, or your podcast host's transcription
2. **Mark timestamps** — flag the 5-10 best moments while listening or scanning transcript
3. **Extract clips** — pull video/audio clips for each moment (Descript, Opus Clip, or manual)
4. **Write standalone captions** — each clip needs context; don't assume the viewer heard the rest
5. **Add subtitles** — most social video is watched without sound
6. **Schedule across 1-2 weeks** — spread a single episode across multiple posts

**Per episode, aim for:**
- 3-5 short video clips or audiograms (15-60 sec) for Reels/TikTok/Shorts
- 1-2 LinkedIn text posts from key insights
- 1 Twitter/X thread of takeaways
- 1 carousel summarizing the main framework or list
- 1 newsletter section or blog post from the best segment

### Webinar / Live Event → Social Content

| Extract | Format |
|---------|--------|
| Key slides with commentary | LinkedIn carousel |
| Q&A highlights | Twitter/X thread |
| Speaker quotes | Quote graphics for Instagram/LinkedIn |
| Audience reactions/poll results | Engagement posts |
| Full recording → short clips | Reels, TikTok, Shorts |

### Newsletter → Social Content

| Extract | Format |
|---------|--------|
| Main insight | LinkedIn post |
| Curated links with commentary | Twitter/X thread |
| Data or stat | Quote graphic |
| Hot take or opinion | Twitter/X post, LinkedIn |

### Repurposing Workflow

1. **Create pillar content** (blog, video, podcast, webinar, newsletter)
2. **Extract content atoms** (5-10 per piece — quotes, stories, tips, data)
3. **Adapt to each platform** (format, length, and tone)
4. **Write standalone captions** (each post must work without context)
5. **Schedule across the week** (spread distribution, don't dump all at once)
6. **Update and reshare** (evergreen content can repeat every 3-6 months)

### Weekly Planning Template

| Day | LinkedIn | Twitter/X | Instagram |
|-----|----------|-----------|-----------|

2. Write 5 LinkedIn posts
3. Write 3 Twitter threads + daily tweets

## Engagement Strategy

### Daily Engagement Routine (30 min)

1. Respond to all comments on your posts (5 min)
2. Comment on 5-10 posts from target accounts (15 min)
3. Share/repost with added insight (5 min)
4. Send 2-3 DMs to new connections (5 min)

## Analytics & Optimization

### Metrics That Matter

**Awareness:** Impressions, Reach, Follower growth rate

**Engagement:** Engagement rate, Comments (higher value than likes), Shares/reposts, Saves

**Conversion:** Link clicks, Profile visits, DMs received, Leads attributed

### Weekly Review

- Top 3 performing posts (why did they work?)
- Bottom 3 posts (what can you learn?)
- Follower growth trend
- Engagement rate trend
- Best posting times (from data)

### Optimization Actions

**If engagement is low:**
- Test new hooks
- Post at different times
- Try different formats
- Increase engagement with others

**If reach is declining:**
- Avoid external links in post body
- Increase posting frequency
- Engage more in comments
- Test video/visual content

**Schedule:** Core content posts, Threads, Carousels, Evergreen content

## Short-Form Video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts)

Short-form video is the highest-reach format on every major platform. These frameworks apply whether you're creating for TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts.

### Platform Specs

| Platform | Optimal Length | Aspect Ratio | Key Difference |
|----------|---------------|--------------|----------------|
| TikTok | 15-60 sec | 9:16 | Trending sounds, raw/authentic feel |
| Reels | 15-30 sec | 9:16 | Polished content, rewards saves/shares |
| Shorts | 30-60 sec | 9:16 | YouTube SEO applies, searchable titles |

### The 3-Second Rule

You have 3 seconds to stop the scroll. Every video needs three simultaneous hooks:

```
[VISUAL HOOK] + [VERBAL HOOK] + [TEXT OVERLAY]
```

All three should hit in the first second.

### Video Structures

**Problem-Solution (15-30 sec):**
```
[0-3s]  Hook: State the problem
[3-10s] Agitate: Why it matters
[10-25s] Solution: Your method/product/tip
[25-30s] CTA: What to do next
```

**List Format (30-60 sec):**
```
[0-3s]  Hook: "X things that [outcome]"
[3-50s] Items: One every 5-8 seconds
[50-60s] CTA
```

**Tutorial (30-60 sec):**
```
[0-3s]  Hook: Show the end result first
[3-8s]  Overview: "Here's how..."
[8-50s] Steps: Quick, clear instructions
[50-60s] Result + CTA
```

### Caption & Subtitle Best Practices

Captions increase watch time by 25-40%. Most social video is watched without sound.

- **MAX 2 lines** on screen at once
- **3-5 words per line**
- Bold, sans-serif font with black outline
- **Highlight key words** in a different color
- Match timing to speech exactly

Tools: CapCut (free), Descript, Captions.ai, Premiere Pro

### Content Ideas by Type

| Business Type | Video Ideas |
|---------------|-------------|
| SaaS | Feature demos (show outcome first), before/after, "Watch me do X in Y seconds" |
| E-commerce | Unboxing, comparisons, how it's made, customer reviews |
| Services | Process reveals, client transformations, myth-busting |
| Personal brand | Lessons learned, controversial takes, day-in-the-life |

### Common Mistakes

1. **Slow hooks** — don't build up to the point
2. **No text overlay** — many watch without sound
3. **Poor audio** — bad audio kills retention instantly
4. **Too long** — if it can be shorter, make it shorter
5. **No CTA** — tell viewers what to do
6. **Ignoring comments** — engagement in first hour matters
